findings.claim: Over whole games v5 does not cast less or hold back cards in any way that matters. The ~1900 probe decisions where v5 passes but hsearch casts are mostly about timing. Across full games v5 casts at hsearch's rate, and its higher pass_with_cast share comes from the denominator: v5 simply passes less often overall. The passive network was v3; v5 casts at hsearch's level again.
findings.evidence: s25.jsonl, 1600 paired tables, rates per candidate own turn (paired per-game differences, mean ± SE). Casts: v5 1.023 vs hsearch 1.018 (+0.006±0.007). pass_cast (passes while a cast was offered): 0.563 vs 0.573 (−0.042±0.024). pass_with_cast share (pass_cast/passes): 0.232 vs 0.175, paired +0.059±0.010 (n=1495), but total passes are 2.42 vs 3.28 per own turn (−0.88±0.09). The gap is in passes where no cast was offered (1.86 vs 2.71), so the share rises because the denominator shrinks. Earlier nets: v3 pass_cast 0.834 (+0.227±0.027) with casts −0.045±0.007; v4b 0.686 (+0.088) with casts −0.021; v5 is back at hsearch's level. Hand size, paired at the k-th own turn with both pilots' candidates still alive (avoids survivorship): v5 holds +0.05±0.01 (k=3), +0.09±0.02 (k=5), +0.14±0.03 (k=6) and +0.33±0.06 (k=8) cards more. Its library is also 0.15–0.23 cards smaller, so it draws about as many extra cards as it keeps. Probe side, for the 1933 'v5 pass / hsearch cast' decisions: v5 is seen casting the same object id later in 21.0% (a lower bound, since only every 3rd decision is probed). 27% of those later casts fall in the same global turn and 68% within 4 global turns (one round). A further 29.8% are still seen in hand later.
examples: g173 t24: v5 passes on Sol Ring#76 (5 lands, net_v 0.65), hsearch casts it; v5 casts Sol Ring#76 at t27
g311 t19: v5 passes on Sol Ring#273 (4 lands, net_v 0.79), casts it at t27
g1380 t40: v5 passes on Sol Ring#183 (1 land on battlefield, net_v 0.09), casts it at t50
findings.interpretation: The probe statistic is a one-step counterfactual: hsearch is asked fresh in v5's position. It does not show that v5 under-deploys over a game. In its own games hsearch has more decision points per own turn (10.4 vs 9.5) and passes more. The small extra hand (+0.1–0.3 cards) goes with extra card draw (smaller library), not with fewer casts. One caveat: per-own-turn rates are mildly biased because v5 games last longer (11.09 vs 10.52 own turns). That is why the hand and board figures were also paired at a matched own-turn index.

findings.claim: When v5 declines a cast that hsearch makes, it is in a low-stakes spot: late, flooded with mana, few options, and especially when the network already rates the game as won. It is not holding mana: v5 passes least when the spell would tap it out. This restraint does not measurably cost wins.
findings.evidence: Own-turn probe decisions where hsearch casts, P(v5 passes). By stage: turn<20 13.7% (n=2005), 20–35 24.6% (n=3415), ≥36 30.6% (n=2366). By option count: 41.2% with 2 options vs 8–15% with 5 or more. By mana slack (v5's lands at turn start minus the card's mana value): 9.2% when the card needs more mana than the lands give (slack −1), 17.5% at exact tap-out, 27% at slack 2–3, 33.0% at slack ≥6. By v5 net_v (the trend holds within each stage): late game 0.19–0.26 for net_v<0.5, rising to 0.375 (0.90–0.98) and 0.437 (≥0.98). Mid game 0.18–0.24 rising to 0.39. There is no matching rise at net_v near 0 (0.22), so this is not symmetric sigmoid saturation. For activations, P(v5 passes | hsearch activates) falls slightly with net_v (0.56 down to 0.42), so the effect is specific to casts. Overall agreement with hsearch falls from 85.7% (turn<12) to 59.0% (turn≥48) and from 71.5% to 59.5% across net_v bins. Sol Ring is the top card in this class (29): 24 of the 29 have ≥5 lands, and most have only 2 options. Cost check in s25 (snap net_v is the v5 net's value for the candidate seat in every pilot's games): of games reaching net_v ≥0.9 at an own-turn snapshot, v5 wins 95.9% (541 games) vs hsearch 95.7% (422); for ≥0.95, 98.6% vs 97.4%. After first crossing 0.9, wins take 4.3 vs 3.9 global turns (2.7 vs 2.7 after crossing 0.95).
examples: g115 t43: v5 passes, hsearch casts Sol Ring (11 lands, hand 7, net_v 0.91, 2 options)
g1506 t57: v5 passes twice on Sol Ring (16 lands, net_v 1.00)
g949 t36: v5 passes on Sol Ring (12 lands, net_v 0.96)
g521 t31/t33: v5 passes on Sol Ring (7–8 lands, net_v 0.99–1.00)
findings.interpretation: This looks like indifference rather than a deliberate pattern. Once the network judges the game won, or the card adds little to a mana-rich board, the search sees almost no value difference, and the tie goes to pass. It is not the 'don't overextend into a wrath' pattern: no slack-dependent mana saving is visible, and the passes are on cheap cards. The conversion numbers show it is harmless, at worst slowing wins by about 0.4 global turns from the 0.9 threshold. Caveat: v5 reaches winning positions in more games, so the conversion comparison is not perfectly matched.

findings.claim: The largest disagreement mass (pass vs activate in both directions, ~4700 decisions) is mostly symmetric churn on low-impact abilities. The same cards appear on both sides, and per-ability agreement is low even between the two searches. It reflects near-indifference in both valuations, not a consistent v5 style.
findings.evidence: Priority probes (n=30867). v5 pass / hsearch activate: 2744. v5 activate / hsearch pass: 1937. Per (card, ability): both pilots chose the same activation 2158 times; one-sided picks total 6178 (v5-only 2921, hsearch-only 3257). The top cards are on both sides (count v5-pass/hsearch-activate vs v5-activate/hsearch-pass): Whirler Rogue 69/44, Rogue's Passage (4,T: unblockable) 68/39, Clue 37/57, Lightning Greaves 36/50, Sylvan Safekeeper (sacrifice a land: shroud) 36/29, Scavenging Ooze 22/28, Terramorphic Expanse 27/24, Evolving Wilds 29/19, Mishra's Factory 17/19. Activations are 85–87% on v5's own turn in both directions; median global turn 34–35 vs 26 for agreed casts. hbot sides with 'pass' in both cases: 60.5% with v5 in pass/activate, 53.0% with hsearch in activate/pass. Self-agreement at priority is 1.00, so the search is deterministic, and 'self' cannot measure this indifference.
examples: Terramorphic Expanse ab0 (when to crack a fetchland): both 26, v5-only 29, hsearch-only 29
Rogue's Passage ab1: both 45, v5-only 50, hsearch-only 76
Sylvan Safekeeper ab0 (sacrifice a land for shroud): both 18, v5-only 32, hsearch-only 36 — both pilots sometimes burn lands for no visible reason
findings.interpretation: Treat roughly the symmetric part (about 2×1937) as a tie-breaking floor between two value functions on nearly equal options, not as play-style. Only the asymmetric remainder, and the ability classes broken out in the next finding, carry signal. Both pilots making dubious sacrifices (Sylvan Safekeeper, Yahenni) points to a weakness of the shared search and move generator under 25 simulations, not of either leaf.

findings.claim: Within activations there is a clear systematic difference. v5 rarely makes tokens, populates, scries or transforms where hsearch does. It equips more, sacrifices permanents for cards more, and uses planeswalker draw abilities more. hsearch's leaf seems to reward immediate board material, while v5 values card flow and equipment.
findings.evidence: Activation abilities classified by their Forge ability type (from the card scripts in third_party/gorge/.cards/cardsfolder), counted as both / v5-only / hsearch-only. Token: 166 / 49 / 387. CopyPermanent (populate): 27 / 11 / 49. Transform (Incubator): 34 / 13 / 64. Scry (Campus lands, Castle Vantress): 33 / 14 / 76. PutCounterAll: 47 / 20 / 70. Destroy: 16 / 11 / 41. Going the other way, Equip: 313 / 585 / 227. Draw with sacrifice: 42 / 163 / 67. Pump with sacrifice: 33 / 116 / 64. Planeswalker draw: 37 / 57 / 17. Cards (v5-only / hsearch-only): Custodi Soulbinders 6/49, Vorel 8/49, Trostani populate 10/49, Ghave 12/43, Incubator 13/64, Imperious Perfect, Vitu-Ghazi, Trading Post, Retrofitter Foundry, Faerie Formation (hsearch-heavy); Swiftfoot Boots 122/48, Lightning Greaves 97/42, Skullclamp 54/25, Quintorius +1 draw 42/12, Sai 34 v5-only, Commander's Sphere sacrifice 32, Mind Stone sacrifice 17/9, Yahenni sacrificing another creature 40/21. Game level (s25, paired per own turn): activations +0.053±0.017 (+6.7%). Board at the k-th own turn (paired, both alive): creatures −0.16±0.02 (k=5), −0.24±0.03 (k=6). This happens even though creature casts are +0.009±0.005 per own turn, so creatures are leaving play faster. Library −0.15..−0.23 (more draw). Life +0.52±0.16 (k=6), +0.97±0.57 (k=8). v5 re-equips the same equipment within a turn (≥2 sightings at 1/3 sampling) in 18% of its equip turns (Swiftfoot 34/159, Greaves 27/125, Skullclamp 14/66).
examples: g17 t21 and t29: hsearch activates Ghave (remove a counter, make a Saproling); v5 passes (net_v 0.77/0.89)
g1 t27: hsearch populates with Trostani; v5 passes (8 lands, net_v 0.85)
g26 t38: v5 sacrifices Mind Stone to draw; hsearch passes
g57 t54: v5 sacrifices to Yahenni twice in one turn; hsearch passes
g118 t36: v5 equips Swiftfoot Boots where hsearch casts Titania's Chosen / Sol Ring
findings.interpretation: This fits the leaves. hsearch's leaf (life + 2*hand + material) rises immediately from a new token or counter and falls from any sacrifice cost. The learned value has apparently discounted cheap tokens and prices card advantage and equipment (haste, hexproof) higher. Skullclamp loops and protective Boots and Greaves are known strong patterns. Some sacrifices (Yahenni into an empty threat, Mind Stone late) look dubious, and repeated Swiftfoot re-equips cost mana. The style is plausibly part of v5's edge, but nothing here proves which activations help. An ablation would be needed.

findings.claim: v5 casts its commander from the command zone more often, mostly by recasting it after removal. This is the cleanest game-level difference in casting behaviour, and it appeared with self-play (v4b and v5).
findings.evidence: s25, commander casts per own turn: v5 0.142 vs hsearch 0.123 (paired +0.018±0.002, about +15%). Per game: 1.577 vs 1.294. Paired over games where both pilots had ≥8 own turns: +0.286±0.034 (n=1264). P(≥1 commander cast) is 90.2% vs 88.1%, but P(≥2) is 42.1% vs 29.1% and P(≥3) 16.9% vs 8.9%. By net: v3 P(≥2) 34.1% (per own turn −0.001±0.002 vs hsearch), v4b 41.1% (+0.016±0.002), v5 42.1%. hbot: 29.3%.
findings.interpretation: Recasting the commander despite the tax is standard Commander play. A value net trained on outcomes can learn that a commander on the battlefield is worth more than the material-based leaf credits. An alternative explanation is that v5's commander dies or gets exiled more often, for example through more aggressive attacks or v5's lower creature counts, which creates more recast opportunities. s25 does not record commander deaths, so the two cannot be separated here. v5 also lives longer (11.09 vs 10.52 own turns), but the per-own-turn rate controls for that.

findings.claim: When both search pilots cast but pick different spells (1716 decisions), v5 more often picks the cheaper, non-creature or ramp spell and leaves the creature for later. hsearch picks the creature.
findings.evidence: Different-cast probes with both cards found in the card scripts. v5's card has lower mana value in 49.7%, equal in 26.4%, higher in 23.9% (mean difference −0.65). Creature share is 52.7% for v5's choice vs 75.8% for hsearch's. Mana rocks 159 vs 53, sorceries 213 vs 136, enchantments 171 vs 77. Top v5 picks: Commander's Sphere 23, Sol Ring 21, Arcane Signet 15. Top hsearch picks: T'Challa 18, Rampaging Baloths 17, Breya 14. These decisions are 100% on v5's turn, median global turn 27. hbot agrees with v5's exact card in only 25%. v5 is seen casting hsearch's card later in ≥26.5% of cases, 12.3% of those in the same global turn. Related: 'v5 activates where hsearch casts' (594) is mostly equipping (Boots 63, Greaves 37, Battle-Axe 27, Skullclamp 24) or a planeswalker ability (Freyalise 35, Quintorius 43) before the cast. Here 43% of the observed later casts come in the same global turn, so it is mainly ordering within a turn.
examples: g49 t11: v5 casts Selesnya Signet, hsearch casts Suture Priest (2 lands)
g40 t4: v5 casts Birds of Paradise, hsearch casts Sol Ring
g69 t44: v5 equips Lightning Greaves, hsearch casts Lingering Souls
findings.interpretation: Ramp first and cheaper spells first are known good sequencing in Commander, since they often let both spells resolve over the turn or the next. Equipping before casting the new creature is neutral to slightly wrong: the new creature then cannot get the haste or protection that turn. This finding is weaker than the commander and activation ones because the counterfactual card is often never seen cast (51.7% never observed again).

findings.claim: Null result: v5 does not hold instants for opponents' turns or play more at instant speed. On opponents' turns it is slightly more passive than hsearch, and the instant disagreements on its own turn are symmetric.
findings.evidence: Priority probes on opponents' turns (n=3750): v5 passes 85.8%, hsearch 80.3%, hbot 54.1%. Instant or flash casts: v5 85 (2.3%), hsearch 115 (3.1%). Activations: 444 vs 615. On v5's own turn, instant or flash casts: v5 663, hsearch 744. Symmetry: when hsearch casts an instant on v5's turn, v5 passes 53.1% (n=495); when v5 casts one, hsearch passes 44.1% (n=526). v5 favours Swords to Plowshares (18) and Path to Exile (11) where hsearch passes; hsearch favours Putrefy, Mortify, Krosan Grip, Fresh Meat where v5 passes. Of about 263 own-turn instants v5 declined, only 19 are seen cast later on an opponent's turn (50 on its own turn). Game level: spells (instants and sorceries) +0.012±0.003 per own turn.
findings.interpretation: Both value functions are close to indifferent about removal timing at 25 simulations. Neither one evaluates holding up interaction, which may need a deeper horizon or opponent modelling that the leaf cannot provide. The extra passes on opponents' turns come from fewer activations, not from held spells.

findings.claim: Null result: land plays and land-versus-spell order never differ. Every probed land decision was identical across v5, hsearch and hbot, and no decision had one pilot play a land while another did something else.
findings.evidence: Priority probes: 5469 land plays with v5 = hsearch = hbot on the exact card (100%). Zero decisions in any class where one pilot's action was a land and another's was not. s25: land plays per own turn are v5 0.926 vs hsearch 0.925 (paired +0.002±0.003). Lands on battlefield, paired at the k-th own turn, differ by ≤+0.07.
findings.interpretation: Land sequencing cannot explain any of v5's gain. The perfect agreement, including with hbot, suggests land plays are effectively fixed by the shared move generator or default policy. I did not check this in the code, so treat land plays as untested by this comparison rather than as evidence that the nets agree.

open_questions: Is v5's extra commander recasting a valuation choice, or a consequence of its commander dying more often? Logging commander zone changes per game would settle it.
Do the token-avoidance and equip/sacrifice-for-cards activation styles cause v5's edge? This needs an ablation, e.g. forcing hsearch's choice on Token-type activations within v5 games.

The probes do not record phase (precombat or postcombat main) or the available options and mana. With those, one could test whether v5's passes are 'cast after combat' sequencing and whether it ends turns with unused mana.

Self-agreement is 1.00 at priority, so the search is deterministic and gives no noise floor for near-indifferent options. Probes with a different search seed for v5 would separate tie-breaking from real preference in the symmetric activation churn.
Is the perfect land-play agreement structural (land plays forced or ordered by the move generator)? Worth checking in the search code before drawing conclusions about land sequencing.

verdicts.recomputed: s25.jsonl, 1600 paired tables. Own turns = own-turn snapshots with the candidate alive (v5 17745, hsearch 16839 in total; mean 11.09 vs 10.52 per game). Paired per-game rate differences (count/own turns), v5 minus hsearch: casts +0.006±0.007, pass_cast -0.042±0.024, passes -0.882±0.090, creatures +0.009±0.005, spells +0.012±0.003, non-creature permanents -0.016±0.003, lands +0.002±0.003. The claim's absolute levels are pooled ratios of sums. I reproduce them exactly: casts 1.023/1.018, pass_cast 0.563/0.573, passes 2.42/3.28, decisions 9.51/10.45. Per-game means are lower (casts 0.998/0.993, passes 2.26/3.14, passes with no cast offered 1.75/2.58). pass_cast/passes share: pooled 0.232 vs 0.175, paired +0.059±0.010 (n=1495). v3: casts -0.045±0.007, pass_cast +0.227±0.027. v4b: casts -0.021±0.007, pass_cast +0.088±0.026. Paired at the k-th own turn with both alive: hand +0.05±0.01 (k=3, n=1600), +0.09±0.02 (k=5), +0.14±0.03 (k=6), +0.33±0.06 (k=8, n=1264), +0.16±0.09 (k=10, n=774). Library -0.15, -0.17, -0.23 at k=5,6,8, but +0.21±0.17 at k=10. Probes: 1933 'v5 pass / hsearch cast' decisions. v5 later casts the same object id in 21.0%. Of those later casts, 27.3% fall in the same global turn and 68.2% within 4 or fewer global turns (48.5% within fewer than 4). Another 29.8% are seen later only as an alternative pilot's cast, i.e. still in hand.
verdicts.reason: Every key number reproduces. The pass_with_cast share does rise because total passes shrink while pass_cast per own turn does not rise, and v3 was the passive net. Three corrections. (1) The levels quoted are pooled ratios while the differences are per-game paired means. That is why 0.563 vs 0.573 (gap -0.010) sits next to a paired -0.042, which is itself only 1.7 SE from zero. (2) Total casts are equal, but the mix shifts: about 6% fewer non-creature permanents, offset by more creatures and instants/sorceries. (3) The paired-at-k comparison avoids survivorship only partly: by k=8 it conditions on the 1264 tables where both pilots survived. The library gap is not stable at k=10 (it flips to +0.21±0.17, not significant). So 'draws as many extra cards as it keeps' holds for k=5 to 8 only.
verdicts.correction: State that levels are pooled (sum/sum) and differences are paired per-game means. pass_cast is not significantly lower (-0.042±0.024). Add that the cast mix shifts (non-creature permanents -0.016±0.003 per own turn, spells +0.012±0.003) while total casts are unchanged. Limit the 'extra hand matched by extra draw' statement to own turns 5 to 8.

verdicts.recomputed: Own-turn priority probes where hsearch casts: n=7932. P(v5 pass): turn<20 13.7% (n=2042), 20-35 24.6% (n=3482), >=36 30.5% (n=2408). By option count: 2 options 41.1% (n=1973), 3 options 25.4%, 4 options 18.7%; 5 to 9 options 8.5%, 11.7%, 13.2%, 18.7%, 18.2%; pooled >=5 12.2% (n=2711). Slack is v5's lands at turn start minus the MV of hsearch's card, MV parsed from ManaCost in the card scripts; 79 MDFC rows unmatched. Results: slack <=-1 9.2% (n=1480; exactly -1 8.8%), 0 17.5%, 1 21.4%, 2-3 27.0%, 4-5 27.3%, >=6 33.0%. net_v bins, late game: 0.21 / 0.26 / 0.25 / 0.27 / 0.33 / 0.375 (0.9-0.98) / 0.437 (>=0.98). Mid game: 0.18 to 0.24, rising to 0.39 at >=0.98. net_v<0.1: 0.21. The net_v trend survives stratification. Within option count, 2 options: 35.9% for net_v<0.5 vs 55.6% for >=0.9; 5+ options: 7.8% vs 22.1%. Within slack 4+: 25.4% vs 40.2%. Activations, P(v5 pass | hsearch activates): 0.58 falling to 0.42. Priority agreement with hsearch: 85.9% (turn<12) to 61.3% (turn>=48); 72.0% to 60.2% across net_v bins. Sol Ring: 29 cases, 24 with >=5 lands, 21 with 2 options. s25 conversion, net_v>=0.9 at an own-turn snapshot: v5 95.9% (541 games) vs hsearch 95.7% (422). At >=0.95: 98.6% (424) vs 97.4% (306). Global turns to the win: 4.33 vs 3.91, and 2.72 vs 2.69. Paired, tables where both crossed 0.9: 96.2% vs 95.0% (n=260).
verdicts.reason: The direction and nearly every figure reproduce. Stratifying by option count and by slack rules out the obvious confounds (more options early, mana-rich late), which makes the claim stronger. Four corrections. (1) At >=5 options the range is 8.5-18.7%, not 8-15%. (2) v5 passes least when its lands alone cannot pay for the card (slack<0, 9.2%), not at tap-out, which is 17.5%. 'Passes least when it would tap out' is wrong. 'No mana-holding pattern' is right, since passing rises steadily with slack. (3) Agreement at turn>=48 is about 61%, not 59.0%. (4) 'Does not measurably cost wins' rests on conversion rates near a 96% ceiling. With n=260 paired tables the SE is about 1.3 pp, so the test can only rule out large costs. The conversion samples are also selected by v5's own net_v.
verdicts.correction: P(v5 pass) is 12.2% pooled at >=5 options (range 8.5-18.7%). It is lowest when the card costs more than v5's lands (9.2%), with 17.5% at exact tap-out, rising to 33% at slack >=6. The net_v effect holds within option-count and slack strata. Conversion after net_v>=0.9 is 95.9% vs 95.7%; this rules out a large cost, not a small one.

verdicts.recomputed: Priority probes n=30867. pass/activate 2744, activate/pass 1937. Per (card, ability), exact-match agreement 2158; one-sided v5 2921 (=1937+594+390), hsearch 3257 (=2744+123+390). Per-card counts (v5 pass & hsearch activate / v5 activate & hsearch pass): Whirler Rogue 69/44, Rogue's Passage 68/39, Clue token 37/57, Lightning Greaves 36/50, Sylvan Safekeeper 36/29, Scavenging Ooze 22/28, Terramorphic 27/24, Evolving Wilds 29/19, Mishra's Factory 19/21. Per-ability splits: Terramorphic ab0 26/29/29, Rogue's Passage ab1 45/50/76, Safekeeper ab0 18/32/36. Share on v5's own turn: 84.6% / 86.9%. Median global turn 34 / 35, vs 26 for agreed casts. hbot passes in 60.5% / 53.0%. Self agreement 1.00. Card-matched symmetry over all 4681 pass-vs-activate decisions: sum over cards of min(count_a, count_b) = 1268 per side, so 2536 decisions (54%) are card-symmetric and 2145 (46%) are card-asymmetric. Largest one-sided cards: Incubator +44 hsearch-side, Custodi Soulbinders +41, Vorel +39, Angel of the Ruins +38, Trostani +36; junk token sac -40 v5-side, Professional Face-Breaker -29, Commander's Sphere -27, Sai -25.
verdicts.reason: The raw counts reproduce, apart from Mishra's Factory (19/21, not 17/19). The 'symmetric floor of about 2x1937' (83% of the mass) overstates it: that measure only compares direction totals. Matched card by card, only 54% of the pass/activate mass is symmetric. The second-largest pass/activate cards (Incubator 51, Custodi 46, Vorel 45, Trostani 39) are strongly one-sided, and they are the token makers of the next finding. Self = 1.00 at priority means the noise floor cannot be measured, as the finding says.
verdicts.correction: About half (54%, 2x1268 of 4681) of the pass-vs-activate disagreement is card-symmetric churn. The other 46% is card-asymmetric and carries the token-vs-equip/draw signal. Mishra's Factory is 19/21.

verdicts.recomputed: Card-level priority counts as both / v5-only / hsearch-only, with 'both' meaning the same card and ability index. Custodi 19/6/49, Vorel 10/8/49, Trostani 27/10/49, Ghave ab0 19/12/43 (but ab1 1/16/4), Incubator token 37/10/61, Imperious Perfect 13/1/36, Vitu-Ghazi 7/1/33, Faerie Formation 18/7/29. Trading Post ab1 5/4/31 but ab0 3/14/1. Retrofitter ab1 5/1/32 but ab0 1/11/6. Going the other way: Swiftfoot 78/122/48, Greaves 61/97/42, Skullclamp 33/54/25, Quintorius ab0 32/42/12, Sai 4/34/2, Commander's Sphere sac 7/32/3, Mind Stone sac 5/17/9, Yahenni 11/40/21. All Equipment-type cards: 334/605/238. Re-equip, defined as ≥2 v5 sightings of the same equipment object in one global turn: 140 of 764 equip turns (18.3%); Swiftfoot 34/159, Greaves 27/125, Skullclamp 14/66. s25 paired: activations +0.053±0.017 per own turn, creature casts +0.009±0.005; creatures at own turn k=5 -0.16±0.02, k=6 -0.24±0.03; library -0.15 to -0.23; life k=6 +0.52±0.16, k=8 +0.97±0.57. In 'v5 activates where hsearch casts' (594), Freyalise accounts for 48 and Quintorius 43.
verdicts.reason: The direction and the card-level magnitudes reproduce. I did not reimplement the Forge ability-type classifier. Equipment by card type (334/605/238) agrees with the claimed Equip class (313/585/227), and every named card matches within a few counts (Incubator 10/61 vs 13/64). Plan replay is not an issue at priority (self agreement 1.00). Three nuances. Some cards are split by ability: Ghave's sacrifice-for-counter ability, Trading Post ab0 and Retrofitter ab0 are v5-heavy. Part of v5's equip surplus is the within-turn re-equip churn the finding itself notes (18% of equip turns), so 'equips more' partly means 'moves equipment more'. The life gain at k=8 is only 1.7 SE from zero.
verdicts.correction: Note that the split is per ability, not per card: v5 favours Ghave's and Trading Post's/Retrofitter's other abilities. Part of the equip surplus is repeated re-equipping within a turn. Incubator is about 10/61. Freyalise in the activate-vs-cast class is 48, not 35.

verdicts.recomputed: s25 commander casts per own turn, paired: v5 +0.018±0.002, v4b +0.016±0.002, v3 -0.001±0.002. Pooled per own turn 0.142 vs 0.123. Per game: v5 1.578, hsearch 1.294, v3 1.345, v4b 1.552, hbot 1.147. Paired over tables where both had >=8 own turns: +0.286±0.034 (n=1264). P(>=1) / P(>=2) / P(>=3): v5 90.2/42.1/16.9%, hsearch 88.1/29.1/8.9%, v3 83.8/34.1/11.8%, v4b 90.1/41.1/16.3%, hbot 68.5/29.3/11.2%. P(>=2 | >=1): v5 46.7%, hsearch 33.0%. findings.interpretation: The search with the hand-made leaf rewards chip damage directly (opponent life is in the leaf). The net appears to value keeping creatures home in the four-player phase, either as untapped blockers or to avoid bad trades. The heads-up null fits that: with one opponent left there is no third party to punish a tapped-out board. The trait cannot by itself explain v5's gain over hsearch, because v3 shows the same restraint (0.421) yet ties hsearch on wins (38.7% vs 38.8%). What v4b/v5 add is in the findings below. Selection caveat: probes only cover positions v5 reached, but hsearch and hbot were asked at those same positions, so the comparison is paired.

findings.claim: When v5 does attack, it commits more of its board than hsearch. The result is fewer, wider swings. The 'continue attacking' part of the probe signal is inflated by plan replay, but a real residual remains with large boards. The two opposite effects cancel at the per-decision level: the overall disagreement split is symmetric.

Part of 'more attackers per attack turn' is a selection effect, because v5 skips small-board turns, which raises its offered count per attack turn. The attackers/offered rate (+3.7 points) is the cleaner measure. The v3-to-v5 rise in width and damage is the combat change that tracks the win-rate gain, unlike the restraint, which v3 already had.

findings.claim: v5 directs its damage away from the opponent with the biggest board and toward the one with the smallest. hsearch is the outlier among the pilots: it hits the biggest board far more than hbot does. Each self-play round moves the nets further from that. hsearch's apparent 'retaliation' against whoever hit it last round turns out to be the same biggest-board effect.

The effect holds when v5's board is at least as big as every opponent's (0.249 vs 0.347, -0.098 [-0.131,-0.066]) and when it is not (0.233 vs 0.381). findings.interpretation: The likeliest mechanism is the hand-made leaf's 'own minus strongest opponent' term. It pays the search for damaging the strongest opponent even when doing so runs into its blockers. The net drops that bias and reverts toward hbot's rule in hbot/combat.go: attack a defender only where block risk is low, ties to lowest life. Alternative explanation: the measure is conditioned on damage landing. Attacks into a big board get blocked more, so a pilot that attacks less often with small boards could show this pattern mechanically. The stratification by relative board size reduces that concern but cannot rule it out.

The s25.json summary fields attack_target_by_life and attack_target_by_power should not be read as defender preferences without conditioning on living opponents and excluding ties.

findings.claim: In the four-player phase, v5 eliminates opponents less often even when it has lethal power on board against one. Heads-up, it closes out games at least as well as hsearch.
findings.evidence: Snapshots plus exit records. An opponent counts as 'in range' when its life is <= the candidate's total creature power at turn start; a kill means that opponent's exit turn equals this turn. With 3 opponents alive and one in range: eliminated that turn v5 0.173 vs hsearch 0.260, -0.087 [-0.123,-0.049] (762 vs 780 turns); hbot 0.257, v3 0.209, v4b 0.160. With 1 opponent left and in range: 0.605 vs 0.576, +0.030 [-0.023,+0.087] (955 vs 860 turns). How often an opponent is in range does not differ: 0.147 vs 0.146 of own turns. Eliminations per own turn with 3 opponents alive: 0.013 vs 0.020 (-0.007 [-0.010,-0.004]). Over the whole game: 0.066 vs 0.069 (n.s.). Exit records: life-total kills on own turn per game 0.814 vs 0.744 (+0.070 [+0.023,+0.120]); the extra kills are final blows in games v5 wins.
findings.interpretation: Possibly learned table politics: as one seat against three hbots, removing the first opponent does not raise its own win probability much, and tapping out to do it exposes the board. It may also just follow from the attack restraint, since 'in range' uses total power and ignores blockers, so some of these kills were not actually available. It was already present in v3/v4b. Caveat: power is a crude lethal proxy, and non-combat kills are mixed in.

findings.claim: The payoff of the restraint shows up on opponents' turns. v5 loses less life per opponent turn even though opponents bring more power, and it dies to life loss less often. Its blocking propensity per decision does not differ in any clear way from hsearch; the gain looks like deterrence from untapped creatures.

Blocks per block step: 0.734 vs 0.671 (+0.063 [+0.016,+0.114]), but v3 is at 0.798, so there is no monotone trend. Blocker probes (n=1873): the v5 pilot answers 'done' 0.511, its fresh self 0.428, hsearch 0.448. The pilot's extra 'done' is plan replay (v5-done/self-block 0.100 vs the reverse 0.017). Fresh v5 blocks about as often as hsearch. Disagreement with hsearch is 0.374 against a self noise floor of 0.141, split both ways: v5 blocks where hsearch would not 0.117 (noise 0.017); v5 declines where hsearch blocks 0.180 (noise 0.100). findings.interpretation: hbot's attacker logic (hbot/combat.go chooseAttackers) skips a defender when blockRisk <= 0 unless the attack is lethal. Keeping creatures untapped therefore directly deflects hbot attacks onto other seats. That fits lower damage per unit of opponent power together with more block steps. The blocker-level differences are real but go in both directions, so the network's distinctive play is about which blocks to make, not how many. Caveat: this conclusion is specific to hbot opponents and may not hold against other opponents.

open_questions: The defender of each attack is not logged in probes (lab.Describe prints 'attack with X' without the target), so 'attack vs attack, different defender' cannot be measured. Same creature at a different defender even counts as agreement. Adding the target to Describe and re-running probes would turn the defender findings from snapshot inference into direct evidence.

The first-step subset is identified heuristically (n_options-1 equal to living opponents times creatures at turn start). It misses first steps with summoning-sick creatures or planeswalker defenders. Logging the declaration step index would remove the guess.

Does the attack restraint actually help? v3 has the same restraint but no win-rate gain. An ablation that forces hsearch's attack/no-attack decision at the first step but keeps the v5 leaf elsewhere would show whether the restraint or the wider swings and target choice drive the v4b/v5 gain.

Is the reduced early elimination a learned 'don't kill the first hbot' policy or a by-product of restraint? It needs a lethal-through-blockers check, which requires per-creature power and toughness that are not in the snapshots.
How much of the defensive gain comes from hbot's blockRisk-based target choice (an opponent-specific exploit)? It needs evaluation against a different opponent policy, or v5 in several seats.

The analyst notes that attack descriptions omit the defender, so same_* only compares which attacker was declared, in which order, or 'done'; that evidence should be dropped. findings.claim: The clearest bad pattern: v5 points harmful effects at its own permanents about twice as often as hsearch, and three times as often as hbot. This is concentrated in repeatable damage abilities ('deals N damage to any target'). Plain destroy/exile removal barely differs.
findings.evidence: Replay, target decisions whose source effect is removal, damage or debuff (n=713). v5 targets its own non-token permanent or itself 140 times (19.6%), hsearch 68 (9.6%), hbot 42 (5.9%). Paired over the same decisions: 92 where only v5 hits itself vs 20 where only hsearch does. Damage effects alone (n=264): own non-token target v5 32%, hsearch 11%, hbot 7%. Destroy/exile removal (n=449): 11% / 8% / 5%. By source, v5 own targets vs hsearch own targets out of n: Ghirapur Aether Grid 25 vs 0 of 55; Zacama's 3-damage ability (ability 0) 13 vs 0 of 27, 7 of the 13 lethal by base toughness; Ion Storm 10 vs 2 of 22; Pia and Kiran Nalaar 6 vs 0 of 8; Hawkeye 5 vs 1 of 14; Hex 6 vs 1 of 30. Most pings are not lethal: Aether Grid 0 of 25 and Ion Storm 0 of 10 hit a creature with base toughness at or below the damage. Self-agreement at target decisions is 0.999, so this is not search noise.
examples: g455 t38 (Zacama, own seat 1): v5 deals 3 damage to its own Zacama#198 and its own Kinjalli's Sunwing#145 (2/3, lethal); hsearch and hbot both target the opponent's Skycat Sovereign#379
g197 t47 (Tinker Time): Ghirapur Aether Grid pings v5's own Sharding Sphinx#278, Whirler Rogue#298 and Gimbal#229 (twice); hsearch and hbot hit the opponent's Raging Swordtooth#71 every time
g1346 t31/t37: Pia and Kiran Nalaar sacrifices an artifact to deal 2 to v5's own Gimbal#129, then to Pia and Kiran#170 itself; hsearch and hbot target the opponent's Metalwork Colossus#247
g1146 t43: Ion Storm hits v5's own Alharu#2 and Bright-Palm#7; hsearch and hbot target the opponent's Ancient Stone Idol#201
g1499 t33: Hex (destroy six target creatures) takes v5's own Angelic Sell-Sword#0 and Captain Lannery Storm#11 while the opponent's Dragonlord Dromoka#316 was available (hsearch and hbot took it)
findings.interpretation: The likely cause is that v5's value net barely separates a small, temporary damage event on its own creature from the same event on an opponent's creature: damage that does not kill leaves the features almost unchanged. With 25 simulations and uniform priors, near-ties then decide the target. The cost is mostly wasted activations (mana, a sacrificed artifact, Ion Storm counters); in the Zacama and Hex cases it kills v5's own creatures. hsearch avoids this even though its leaf is just as blind to non-lethal damage, perhaps because its 'own minus strongest opponent' term rewards anything that weakens opponents within the rollout. Alternatives considered: (a) a mixed-up source, for example Predator, Flagship, whose 'gains flying' ability sat in the removal bucket until I classified per ability index; after that fix the pattern remains, carried by single-effect damage cards. (b) Selection: only 64 games are affected, and those decisions come from games v5 won 59% of the time vs 65% for all harm decisions, which is weak and confounded. The arena win-rate gain clearly does not come from this behaviour.

findings.claim: v5 is less 'political' than hsearch, not more. When both target an opponent but different ones, hsearch goes for the board or material leader much more often. On the life leader they do not differ (null).
findings.evidence: Main probes, target decisions where v5 and hsearch both picked an opponent's object or player, but different opponents, with at least 2 opponents alive (n=370). Rank by the turn snapshot: power leader hit by hsearch 50.8% vs v5 33.5% (bottom-power opponent 28.1% vs 40.8%). Material leader (life + 2*hand + lands + creatures + power) 53.0% vs 35.7%. Life leader 43.0% vs 42.2%, no difference. Against hbot (n=412): power leader 48.5% vs v5 38.8%, life leader 41.0% vs 41.3%. Replay restricted to removal/damage/debuff (n=105): material leader hsearch 61% vs v5 19%, power leader 55% vs 27%, life leader 50% vs 37%. When both pick an opponent, they pick the same opponent in 67.5% of multi-opponent cases (1,140).
examples: g197 t47-53: hsearch and hbot keep hitting the biggest opposing threats (Raging Swordtooth, Pantlaza, Kinjalli's Sunwing) while v5 spreads its targets or turns them on itself
g1124 t30: Hawkeye's ping: hsearch and hbot target God-Eternal Bontu#226 (5/6); v5 pings its own Captain America#8
findings.interpretation: The likely mechanism lies in the hand-made leaf: sigmoid((own - strongest opponent)/20) only rewards damage to the strongest opponent, so hsearch is structurally a leader-hitter. v5 gets the hand-made leaf as an input feature but evidently learned no strong 'hurt the leader' term. Its choices among opponents look close to uniform (top 33.5 / bottom 40.8 by power, about 33/33/33 by chance with three opponents). Life-leader rates match, so the difference is about board strength, not life totals. The snapshot is taken at the start of the turn, not at the moment of decision: a small source of noise, but the same for both pilots.

findings.claim: The same lean toward own targets is useful on beneficial effects that hbot misreads. On auras, pump and keyword grants, v5 targets its own creatures more often, and on cards like Predator, Flagship, Whirler Rogue and Peema Aether-Seer much more often than hsearch.
findings.evidence: Replay, pump/counter effects (n=742), own non-token target: v5 61%, hsearch 53%, hbot 39%. Auras (n=156): 73% / 64% / 22% (hbot puts Rancor and Vow of Lightning on opponents' creatures; both searches correct that, and v5 ≈ hsearch there). By card, own targets v5 / hsearch / hbot: Predator ability 0 ('target creature gains flying') 82 / 7 / 0 of 135; Whirler Rogue (can't be blocked) 33 / 14 / 2 of 200; Rogue's Passage 33 / 23 / 1 of 128; Peema Aether-Seer 8 / 1 / 1 of 10; Mina and Denn 16 / 9 / 4 of 30. In the main probes, at slots where hbot picked an opponent (n=1,812), v5 targets its own permanent 22.5% vs hsearch 18.7% (paired 180 vs 112). That number mixes the harmful damage cases with these boons.
examples: Predator, Flagship (replay, 135 activations): v5 gives flying to its own attackers in 82; hsearch and hbot give it to opponents' creatures in 103 and 109 (useful only to set up the 5-mana destroy ability, which was activated 8 times)
Whirler Rogue: 'target creature can't be blocked' goes on an opponent's creature for hbot 173/200 and hsearch 161/200, which is pointless outside v5's combat; v5 still does it 151/200 but less often
findings.interpretation: v5 has a broad lean toward targeting its own side, applied to good and bad effects alike. That fits a value function that likes 'my creatures were touched', or one that cannot tell polarity for low-impact effects, better than one with a real model of each card. Where hbot's targeting rule defaults to foreign targets for effects it does not understand, the lean helps; on pings it hurts. hbot polarity is only a proxy: hbot leads with foreign targets for any effect it does not know as a boon.

findings.claim: Among its own creatures, v5 picks smaller ones for equipment and pumps than hsearch or hbot does. Equip activations, about a quarter of all target decisions, are a low-stakes, high-volume source of disagreement inflated by re-equipping.
findings.evidence: Main probes, base power (Forge PT) of the target when both pick a creature on the same side and differ. Slots where hbot picked own: v5 minus hsearch -0.35 (v5 larger in 142, smaller in 184, n=408); v5 minus hbot -0.68 (142/246). Slots where hbot picked an opponent: -0.45 vs hsearch (132/177), -1.39 vs hbot (92/266). Replay, equip (n=1,458, 25% of all 5,843 targets, about 24% of target disagreements): -0.56 vs hsearch (225/327). Swiftfoot Boots / Lightning Greaves -0.80 (93/178). Destroy/exile removal vs hsearch: +0.11 (38/29), no difference. Equip churn: 1,474 equip activations in 300 games; in 186 of 630 equipment-turns the same equipment was activated 4 times. 513 activations (35%) re-equip onto the creature already carrying it. At those 513 priority decisions hsearch would pass 131 times and repeat the activation 175 times; hbot would repeat it 265 times.
examples: g22 t41: v5 activates Blade of the Bloodchief#303's equip four times onto Oathsworn Vampire#334 in one turn; hsearch passes at 3 of the 4
g2 t25: Cranial Plating re-equipped onto the same thopter token; hsearch passes
findings.interpretation: The re-equip loop comes mainly from the hbot default policy (hbot repeats it at 52% of these decisions); v5 keeps more of it than hsearch does. It burns spare mana and is mostly harmless, but it inflates the target-disagreement count, because the alternative pilot asked at the follow-up target decision picks some other creature. Preferring smaller creatures for Boots/Greaves (hexproof, haste) is probably slightly worse, as the commander or the biggest threat is the usual choice. There is no evidence that v5 removes smaller opposing creatures than hsearch.

findings.claim: At modal choices, hbot always takes mode 0. Both searches spread over modes, and v5 takes 'mode 2' much more often than hsearch. The largest single difference is Fiery Confluence, where v5 picks 'destroy target artifact' and then partly aims it at its own artifacts.
findings.evidence: Main probes, modes n=383, self-agreement 99.5%. v5: mode 0 152, mode 1 152, mode 2 52, mode 3 10, done 17. hsearch: 164 / 160 / 15 / 8 / done 36. hbot: mode 0 330, done 49. Agreement with v5: hsearch 56.9%, hbot 42.6%. Replay (n=616): Fiery Confluence mode 2 (destroy target artifact) v5 17/18 vs hsearch 0/18 (hsearch: 14 times '1 damage to each creature', 4 times '2 damage to each opponent'). The resulting artifact targets hit v5's own artifacts 5 of 16 times. Requisition Raid (n=50): v5 stops early ('done') 13 times vs hsearch 26. 336 modal choices come from triggers (Land's Wrath, Reap the Tides, Most Wanted, Mardu Surge). There the disagreements are near-symmetric swaps between mode 0 and mode 1 (v5 0 / hsearch 1: 65; v5 1 / hsearch 0: 45). Valorous Stance, Austere Command, Wreck and Rebuild and Return of the Wildspeaker: v5 ≈ hsearch (agreement 9-11 of 11-17).
examples: g1596 t30 (own seat 2): Fiery Confluence, three times 'destroy target artifact'; v5 targets its own Replicating Ring#272 and its own Bloodforged Battle-Axe#202 (hsearch's targets: a thopter token)
g1308 t29 (seat 0): Fiery Confluence destroys v5's own Gruul Signet#30
findings.interpretation: The modes data are thin (383 probes) and mostly come from a handful of decks. Apart from Fiery Confluence, where v5's mode choice links up with the own-target pattern of finding 1, the differences are swaps between mode 0 and mode 1 with no clear direction, a plausible near-tie under 25 simulations.

findings.claim: Null result: choose decisions barely differ. They are mostly cost and payment picks (which artifacts to tap, what to sacrifice, which land to fetch, crew). v5 differs only in stopping early ('done') somewhat more often and in discarding cheaper cards.
findings.evidence: Main probes: agreement with hsearch 85.6%, with hbot 83.4%, hsearch vs hbot 87.8%, self 99.6%. Replay (n=5,938): agreement with hsearch 88.0%, hbot 85.6%. By context: scry/surveil 99%, dig 100%, triggered choices 92-93%, sacrifice 81% (n=1,175), discard 72% (n=265). 'done' picks: main data v5 586, hsearch 515, hbot 335. In the replay, v5 picks 'done' where hsearch does not 124 times, the reverse 60 times; the largest sources are crew/tap costs (N'Yami-Class Mother Ship 18, Avengers Quinjet 8). Discard disagreements (n=80 with known costs): v5's discard has mean mana value 2.41 vs hsearch 3.01; type pairs land-vs-creature 10, creature-vs-land 6. Sacrifice disagreements: token-vs-token 52, creature-vs-creature 30; mean mana value 2.65 vs 2.81 (n=94). Numeric picks ('choose N', e.g. X values) appear only twice among the probed choose decisions, so the data cannot answer the X-value question.
examples: Whirler Rogue's cost 'tap two untapped artifacts' accounts for 66 replay choose disagreements: which two artifacts to tap
Quintorius, History Chaser (32 disagreements): which card to discard
findings.interpretation: Choose decisions are mostly low-impact payments where several options are nearly equivalent, so the remaining 12-14% disagreement looks like tie-breaking rather than a style. Stopping early on crew costs leaves vehicles uncrewed, a small possible cost. Nothing here suggests the network systematically sacrifices or discards worse cards.

findings.claim: Null result for one artefact: the low target agreement (47%) is not explained by decided positions where every option looks equally good. It holds across the whole value range and on both players' turns.
findings.evidence: Main probes, v5–hsearch target agreement by net_v: 0.05-0.2: 49.4% (n=480), 0.2-0.5: 47.9% (1,065), 0.5-0.8: 48.4% (1,023), 0.8-0.95: 47.1% (645). Only the extremes are lower: <0.05: 32.6% (193), >0.95: 42.9% (434). Same picture by leaf_v (44.5-50.3% in every bin). v5's turn: 46.4% (n=3,591); opponents' turns: 51.0% (249). Even hsearch and hbot agree only 58-61% at targets.
findings.interpretation: Target disagreement is a property of how the two leaf evaluators rank similar options under a 25-simulation, uniform-prior search, not of lost or won positions. The extremes add some noise. One more caveat: alternatives were asked at v5's target decisions after v5 chose the spell or mode, so hsearch's 'target' answers v5's situation, not a plan of its own.

open_questions: The probes do not record the source of a target, choose or modes decision (FeatSource / Decision.Sub) or the option list. Adding both to study.Probed would make the replay attribution unnecessary and give a random-choice baseline: which targets were even available to v5. Currently 885 of the 5,843 replay targets follow trigger ordering and have no attributed source.

Is the self-pinging fixable by a small rule (never point a 'deal damage' or 'destroy' effect at your own permanent when an opponent's is legal) without losing the useful own-target boons? An arena A/B with this pruning at the target level would show what it is worth.

Why does v5 keep less of the leader focus that the hand-made leaf it receives as input carries? A probe of net_v differences between hitting the strongest and the weakest opponent in matched positions would test whether the net has a leader term at all.

The replay sample (300 games selected for many target/modes probes) over-represents a few decks (Tinker Time, Riders of Rohan, Land's Wrath). The per-card counts above should be confirmed on a random game sample.
The equip churn (35% of equips re-attach to the same creature) is inherited from hbot's priority policy. Does it cost tempo in practice, for example mana not spent on casting?

verdicts.recomputed: I used the analyst's 300-game v5 replay (tmclens/r300.jsonl). Before using it I checked that 299 of its 300 games match s25 v5 outcome, winner, turns and seat, and that object id//100 equals the owner's seat (8321 of 8324 of v5's own casts and land plays). I wrote my own attribution: a target decision counts only if it follows directly from a v5 cast or activate in the same turn. The effect class comes from that ability's Forge script line, including its SubAbility chain. Harmful sources (destroy/exile/damage), n=508. v5 targets its own non-token permanent or itself 105 times (20.7%), hsearch 39 (7.7%), hbot 14 (2.8%). Paired, only v5 does it 81 times vs only hsearch 15. Damage, n=225: 33.8% / 7.6% / 3.1%. Destroy/exile, n=283: 10.2% / 7.8% / 2.5%. By source (v5 own vs hsearch own, of n): Ghirapur Aether Grid 26/0 of 55, in only 2 games. Zacama ability 0: 13/0 of 27, 4 games, 7 of the 13 lethal by base toughness. Ion Storm: 10/2 of 22, 2 games. Pia and Kiran: 6/0 of 8. Hex: 6/1 of 30. Hawkeye: 5/1 of 14. Lethality checks match: Aether Grid 0 of 25, Ion Storm 0 of 10. The top 3 sources supply 47% of v5's own-harm picks. Without them: 13.9% / 9.2% / 3.2% (n=404). By game: v5 has more own-harm picks than hsearch in 28 games, the reverse in 11. 47 games are affected. Those decisions come from games v5 won 59% of the time, vs 67% for all harm decisions. Main-probe target self-agreement is 0.999. By seat, the own-harm rate is 24/21/25/12% for v5 and 12/10/4/5% for hsearch.
verdicts.reason: The direction holds and is large. The magnitudes differ from the claim: with direct attribution, v5 hits itself about 2.7 times as often as hsearch, not twice, and hbot's rate is 2.8%, not 5.9%. The analyst's n=713 also includes looser after-pass attributions. The finding overstates how broad the pattern is. Nearly half of it comes from three repeatable pingers in about 8 games, and outside them the gap shrinks to 13.9% vs 9.2%. It is still significant at game level (28 vs 11). Self-agreement of 0.999 shows the search is deterministic, not that the choice is robust. Own-targeting falls with seat number for both searches (main probes, at slots where hbot targeted an opponent: v5 31.7% at seat 0 vs 13.4% at seat 3). That pattern fits ties being broken by option order, which agrees with the near-tie interpretation. A few 'own' targets are forced by the card and not choices: the first target of a fight spell such as Savage Stomp, or the graveyard card for Vengeful Rebirth. These are about symmetric across pilots.
verdicts.correction: Restate as follows. On directly attributed harmful targets in the replay (n=508), v5 picks its own permanent or itself 20.7% of the time, vs 7.7% for hsearch and 2.8% for hbot (paired 81 vs 15). On damage effects the rates are 33.8% / 7.6% / 3.1%. The effect is concentrated: Aether Grid, Zacama and Ion Storm give 49 of v5's 105 own-harm picks, from about 8 games. Without those three sources the rates are 13.9% vs 9.2%. 47 games are affected, not 64. Self-agreement shows determinism and says nothing about robustness. The seat gradient suggests that option-order tie-breaking contributes.

verdicts.recomputed: Main probes, target decisions where v5 and hsearch both picked an opponent's object or player and at least 2 opponents were alive: n=1140, same opponent in 67.5%. Where they picked different opponents (n=370), I reproduced the analyst's numbers exactly. Power leader: hsearch 50.8% vs v5 33.5%. Bottom-power opponent: 28.1% vs 40.8%. Material leader: 53.0% vs 35.7%. Life leader: 43.0% vs 42.2%. Against hbot (n=412): power leader 48.5% vs 38.8%, life leader 41.0% vs 41.3%. Over all 1140 decisions, not only the differing ones: power leader v5 51.6% vs hsearch 57.2%, material leader 48.3% vs 53.9%, life leader 44.4% vs 44.6%. Picking in proportion to opponents' creature counts would give 56.3%. Replay, directly attributed harmful effects with different opponents (n=82): material leader v5 16% vs hsearch 66%, power leader 27% vs 56%, life leader 35% vs 49%.
verdicts.reason: The direction is reproduced, and it is significant at game level. The 17-point gap exists only in the subset where the two pilots chose different opponents. Over all decisions the gap is about 5.6 points (power leader) and 5.6 points (material leader), so 'much more often' is overstated. Under uniform choice among opponents, 33.5% would be close to chance. Under choice in proportion to creatures, v5 sits below chance and hsearch near it, so hsearch is not clearly 'political' either. In the replay subset of harmful effects, the life-leader rates also differ (35% vs 49%), so the life 'null' holds only in the main probes.
verdicts.correction: The magnitude should be reported over all decisions: power leader 51.6% vs 57.2% and material leader 48.3% vs 53.9% (n=1140), with life leader equal (44.4% vs 44.6%). The 50.8% vs 33.5% figures apply only to the 32.5% of decisions where the two pilots picked different opponents. Hitting the leader at about the rate expected from creature counts is not necessarily political targeting.

findings.claim: Almost all of v5's edge over hsearch:25 comes from not being eliminated. It wins fast games no more often than hsearch does. The extra wins come in long games (more than 12 own turns) that hsearch never reached.
findings.evidence: Paired, 1600 games. Candidate eliminated: hs 58.6% vs v5 51.3% (-7.3 +-2.8 pts). Win rate +6.5 +-2.8 pts (v5-only wins 320, hs-only wins 216). Stalls and fails are flat (3.2% vs 3.8%). Eliminated before own turn 8: -3.8 +-1.7 pts; before 10: -7.0 +-2.3; before 12: -8.0 +-2.5. Won before own turn 8: -0.2 +-0.3; before 10: -0.8 +-1.4; before 12: +0.6 +-2.2 (all null). Won/eliminated/alive at own turn 12: hs 19.2/45.8/32.9%, v5 19.8/37.8/39.6%. Wins as a share of all games: within 12 own turns hs 24.5% vs v5 25.9%; after 12 own turns hs 14.3% vs v5 19.4%. So about 5.1 of the 6.5 pts come from long games. In games both won (n=405), v5 needs 0.34 +-0.27 more own turns. In games where both were eliminated (n=611), v5 dies 0.38 +-0.20 own turns later. Same table, hs eliminated before own turn 9 while v5 won: 84 games; the reverse: 36.
examples: game 37 Klingon Fury (TRC): hs has life 5 and power 4 at own turn 6 and is killed on own turn 7; v5 has life 25 and power 6 at own turn 6 and wins after 14 own turns
game 120 Reap the Tides (CMR): hs is down to life 10 by own turn 6 and dies to commander damage on own turn 6; v5 has life 39 and wins after 11 own turns
game 51 Guided By Nature (C14): hs has life 11 at own turn 6 and dies on own turn 8; v5 has life 30 and power 11 and wins after 9 own turns
game 125 Fae Dominion (WOC): hs dies on own turn 7; v5 wins after 18 own turns
findings.interpretation: The learned leaf mainly buys survival. Turn-k comparisons are paired and count the earlier-dying pilot as dead, so this is not survivorship. The slower wins could be a style choice or just a consequence of games lasting longer: in games both pilots won, the delay is only a third of a turn. The v5 network does not convert faster. It reaches the late game more often, and then wins about as often as hs does from there.

findings.claim: Compared on games where all five pilots are still alive at own turn k, v5 keeps more cards in hand, more life and slightly more lands. It has fewer creatures and less power than hsearch, which dumps its board fastest. Opponents lose life more slowly against v5 early on.
findings.evidence: All-5-alive conditioning (n=1540 at k=6, 1109 at k=8, 776 at k=9), paired v5-hs. Hand: k6 +0.14 +-0.07, k8 +0.35 +-0.12, k9 +0.30 +-0.16. Life: k6 +0.54 +-0.31, k7 +1.06 +-0.45. Lands: k6 +0.06 +-0.03, k7 +0.09 +-0.04. Creatures: k5 -0.16 +-0.04, k6 -0.24 +-0.06, k7 -0.26 +-0.11. Power: k6 -0.77 +-0.22 (hs 6.41, v5 5.63, hbot 4.91), k7 -1.02 +-0.35. Commander damage received: k7 -0.10 +-0.08. Summed opponent life (higher = less damage done): k6 +1.05 +-0.45, k8 +2.61 +-1.08, k9 +2.97 +-1.58. Opponents' max power rises against v5: k8 +0.90 +-0.53, k9 +1.66 +-0.91. Opponents' lands, hands and creature counts are identical across pilots at every k (differences at most 0.1). A pairwise hs/v5-alive check (n=1264 at k=8) agrees: v5 has taken 0.97 less damage, opponents have lost 3.1 +-1.6 less life, v5 has 0.98 less power and +0.33 hand.
examples: game 132 Blood Rites (LCC): at own turn 6 hs has 7 creatures and power 66 and wins on own turn 7; v5 has 0 creatures, life 4, and is eliminated on own turn 6
findings.interpretation: This looks like a value-and-safety trade: v5 commits fewer creatures early, holds cards, and pays for it with less damage dealt and opposing boards growing larger. That it still wins more suggests the hand-made leaf (life + 2*hand + material) used by hsearch overvalues board presence compared with staying alive. The extra hand is not a mulligan artefact (mulligans are 0 for all pilots). Possible cause: more passes with castable cards, per the next finding.

findings.claim: Across rounds, the network kept v3's survival and hand gains but put back the tempo v3 had given up. Every activity measure rose monotonically v3 -> v4b -> v5 along with win rate. v3 is the most passive pilot and only ties hsearch.
findings.evidence: Win: 38.7 -> 42.2 -> 45.3% (paired v3->v4b +3.5 +-2.6, v4b->v5 +3.1 +-2.6). Eliminated: 58.0 -> 55.0 -> 51.3%. Per own turn, whole game: casts 0.970 -> 0.996 -> 1.023 (hs 1.018); passes while a cast was offered 0.834 -> 0.686 -> 0.563 (hs 0.573); activations 0.745 -> 0.792 -> 0.844 (hs 0.786); commander casts 0.124 -> 0.141 -> 0.142 (hs 0.123); attackers 1.237 -> 1.264 -> 1.326 (hs 1.495); opponent life lost per own turn 3.50 -> 3.74 -> 3.96 (hs 4.49); own life lost per opponent turn 0.98 -> 0.99 -> 0.96 (hs 1.02). All-5-alive at k=6: power 4.83 -> 5.20 -> 5.63 (v5-v3 +0.80 +-0.21), creatures 1.74 -> 1.84 -> 1.96, summed opponent life 106.2 -> 105.8 -> 104.8 (v5-v3 -1.40 +-0.40), hand flat at 5.30/5.34/5.29 (-0.01 +-0.07), life 36.15/36.59/36.71. hs vs v3 has the same win rate (-0.1 +-2.7) with a different mix: v3 wins fewer games before own turn 10 (-1.8 +-1.4 pts) and dies a little less.
findings.interpretation: v3 learned that keeping cards and life matters but became passive: it passes with castable cards 46% more often than hs. Self-play rounds moved it back toward spending mana (casts, activations, commander) without giving up hand or life. The per-own-turn rates span whole games and lean on late turns for pilots that survive longer. The k=6 snapshot comparisons, which are survivorship-controlled, move in the same direction.

findings.claim: Search with the hand-made leaf underuses commander damage. All networks finish games by commander damage about as often as hbot does, and more often than hsearch.
findings.evidence: Final blow by commander damage in candidate wins: hbot 10.9% (43/396), hs 6.1% (38/621), v3 10.2% (63/619), v4b 10.2% (69/675), v5 10.6% (77/725). hs vs v5 two-proportion z of about 2.9. Commander casts per own turn: hs 0.123, v5 0.142. Commander-damage kills on the candidate's own turn per game: hs 0.062, v5 0.084 (paired +0.021 +-0.018, marginal). Commander-damage eliminations per game, all players: hs 0.145 vs v5 0.149 (null). The difference is who deals them. Null: the candidate is killed by commander damage in 5.2% (hs, 49/938) vs 5.6% (v5, 46/821) of its eliminations.
findings.interpretation: The hand-made leaf cannot see commander damage (life + hand + material), so search undervalues recasting and pushing the commander. The network has state features that include it. The effect is modest and accounts for only part of the win gain: about 39 of v5's 104 extra wins end with a commander blow.

findings.claim: v5's gain over hsearch varies by deck more than chance allows, and the per-deck pattern partly repeats across network versions. It does not concentrate in strong decks: weak and mid decks gain at least as much. Creature-heavy decks gain least.
findings.evidence: Per deck, paired v5-hs from s25 (n=23-50 games per deck). Permutation heterogeneity test p=0.003 (stat 73.6 vs null mean 43.8). Split-half reliability of per-deck gain r=0.30. Network-specific deck effects with independent noise: corr((v5-hs),(v4b-hbot))=0.34 (perm p=0.015), corr((v5-hs),(v3-hbot))=0.28 (p=0.048). Tercile by hbot-candidate deck win rate: weak (515 games, hbot 9.7%) hs 24.7 -> v5 32.0 (+7.4 +-4.6); mid (553) 39.8 -> 47.4 (+7.6 +-5.1); strong (532, hbot 39.3%) 51.5 -> 56.0 (+4.5 +-4.9). corr(gain, control rate) = -0.16, n.s. Deck covariates measured on hbot-pilot games: corr(gain, hbot creatures at own turn 6) = -0.35 (p=0.02); with commander casts per turn -0.37 (p=0.01); with hbot fast-win share -0.10 (n.s.). Largest gains: Upgrades Unleashed +0.30 +-0.18 (n=33), Reap the Tides +0.30 +-0.17 (30), Breed Lethality CM2 +0.29 +-0.16 (38), Hatsune Miku +0.26 +-0.17 (34), Most Wanted +0.24 +-0.16 (42). Largest losses: Blood Rites -0.31 +-0.17 (36; hs 0.83 vs v5 0.53 and v3 0.36), Witherbloom Pestilence -0.21 +-0.23 (28), Abzan Armor -0.13 +-0.23 (30), Wakanda Forever -0.12 +-0.25 (26).
examples: Blood Rites games 27, 300, 658, 1048: hs wins with power 10-15 at own turn 6, while v5 is at power 5-12 and gets eliminated or stalls
Upgrades Unleashed: hs 0.15, v3 0.33, v4b 0.52, v5 0.45; the gain is already present in v3
findings.interpretation: The networks' more patient style helps most where hsearch was dumping resources into a weak board, and hurts in go-wide or aggro decks (Blood Rites) where hsearch's fast deployment was correct. Only 2 of 45 deck intervals exclude zero, so single-deck claims are weak. The robust facts are that heterogeneity exists, it repeats across nets, and it relates to board-centric decks rather than deck strength. corr(gain, hs rate) = -0.48 is regression to the mean (shared hs noise) and should not be read as a weak-deck effect.

findings.claim: Several game-flow features do not change between hsearch and v5: how it closes games once it wins, who kills it, stall rate, the opponents' development, and the opening 3-4 own turns.
findings.evidence: Last elimination dealt on the candidate's own turn in its wins: hs 96.8% (601/621), v5 98.1% (711/725). Opponent eliminations on own turn per win: hs 2.07, v5 2.02. Candidate killed on its own turn: under 1% for all pilots. Share of candidate deaths dealt by the eventual winner: hs 0.59, v5 0.63. Stalled or failed: hs 3.2%, v5 3.8%. Opponents' lands, hand size and creature count: all-5-alive differences of at most 0.11 at every k up to 10. Own turns 1-4: life and lands identical (|diff| at most 0.11); only the first creature drops differ (power at k4 -0.20 +-0.07). Seat effect: every pilot does best in seat 3 (v5 52.1%, hs 41.7%). Seats are balanced (388-408 games each), so this does not bias the comparison. Total opponent eliminations per game: hs 2.35, v5 2.40. v5 does make 0.098 +-0.058 more own-turn kills per game, consistent with longer survival.
findings.interpretation: The network changes how long the candidate lasts and what it holds, not how games are closed or how hbot opponents develop. Selection is not an issue for these numbers: all comparisons use the same seeds and tables.

findings.claim: Overall plan of the network: survival and value first, tempo second. It trades early board presence and damage for hand cards, life and avoiding the first elimination. Self-play has been adding tempo back while keeping that cushion. v5 sits between passive v3 and board-dumping hsearch on tempo, and above both on survival.
findings.evidence: Synthesis of the findings above. At k=6-8 (survivorship-controlled), v5 vs hs: hand +0.14 to +0.35, life +0.5 to +1.1, power -0.77 to -1.0, opponent life +1 to +3. Eliminated -7.3 pts; wins before own turn 12 unchanged (+0.6 +-2.2); wins after own turn 12 +5.1 pts. v3 -> v5: power at k6 +0.80, casts per turn +5%, passes with a castable card -33%, each step adding about 3 win pts.
findings.interpretation: The 100-simulation results (hs 43.4%, v5 51.4%) are consistent with deeper search amplifying a better long-horizon value, but I did not analyse them here. Alternative explanation: the net may simply value hand cards more than the leaf's 2x weight, and survival follows from not over-extending into hbot's attacks (hbot attacks the highest-life opponent 42% and the highest-power one 47%). Both explanations predict the same curves.

open_questions: Is v5's extra hand made of uncastable cards (colour or mana screw stand-ins, basic-land replacements) or of deliberate holds? The probes file could split pass_cast decisions by whether the held card was castable and by turn.

Are the per-own-turn play rates (casts, pass_cast, activations) the same in a fixed early window (own turns 1-6)? The s25 play counts are whole-game totals, so I could not separate them from the longer-survival mix.
Why does Blood Rites collapse under every network (hs 0.83, v3 0.36, v4b 0.53, v5 0.53)? Is it a lifelink or go-wide feature the network misvalues, or noise (n=36)?
Does the survival advantage hold at 100 simulations, or does the 100-sim gain come more from fast wins? This needs a 100-sim study file.
Opponents keep more power against v5 (+0.9 to +1.7 max opponent power at k8-9). Is this from attacking less often (v5 attacks on 42.3% of own turns vs hs 51.8%) or from fewer removal casts?

Won within 12 own turns (<=12): hs 24.5%, v5 25.9% (+1.44 +-2.48). Won after more than 12: hs 14.3%, v5 19.4% (+5.06 +-2.31). Both won (n=405): v5 takes +0.34 +-0.27 more own turns. Both eliminated (n=611): v5 dies +0.38 +-0.20 own turns later. hs eliminated before own turn 9 while v5 won: 84 games; the reverse: 36. Alive at own turn 12 (neither won nor eliminated by turn 12): hs 26.0%, v5 32.7%. Win rate among those alive: hs 14.3/26.0 = 55%, v5 19.4/32.7 = 59%. verdicts.reason: Every headline number reproduces. Three problems need fixing. (1) 'Comes from not being eliminated' is almost an accounting identity. A candidate who is not eliminated and not stalled has won, so win diff = -(elim diff) - (stall diff): 6.5 = 7.3 - 0.8. The informative part of the finding is the timing split, not the survival framing. (2) 'Long games that hsearch never reached' is false as worded. hs is still alive at own turn 12 in 26.0% of games, against 32.7% for v5. v5 reaches the late game more often and then converts at a similar rate (55% vs 59%). (3) The quoted 'won/eliminated/alive at own turn 12: hs 19.2/45.8/32.9, v5 19.8/37.8/39.6' does not add up. It mixes '<12' counts for won and eliminated with some other definition of alive (100-19.2-45.8 = 35.0, not 32.9). The 'about 5.1 of 6.5 pts' share has wide error bars (+5.1 +-2.3 vs +1.4 +-2.5), so 'most of', not 'almost all', is what the data supports.
verdicts.correction: The win gain shows up as fewer eliminations (an identity given flat stall rates). Its timing: wins within 12 own turns are unchanged (+1.4 +-2.5 pts), and wins after 12 own turns rise by +5.1 +-2.3 pts, roughly three quarters of the gain. hs is still alive at own turn 12 in 26.0% of games and v5 in 32.7%. From there they convert at similar rates (55% vs 59%). Replace 'that hsearch never reached' with 'that hsearch reached less often'. Fix the alive-at-12 figures to 26.0% / 32.7% (definition <=12) or 35.0% / 42.4% (complement of the <12 counts).

Pairwise hs-and-v5-alive at k8 (n=1264): life +0.97 +-1.13, opponent life +2.59 +-1.03 (raw sum +3.12 +-1.55), power -0.98 +-0.60, hand +0.33 +-0.11. Mulligans are 0 for every pilot. Game 132 reproduces (hs 7 creatures, power 66, wins at own turn 7; v5 0 creatures, life 4, eliminated at own turn 6). Per-own-turn whole-game rates, paired per game, v5-hs: casts +0.006 +-0.014; pass_cast -0.042 +-0.047; creatures cast 0.591 vs 0.581.
verdicts.reason: The curve differences reproduce. hs has the largest board of all five pilots at every k from 4 to 10. Three corrections. (a) The life advantage is significant only at k6-7. At k8-9 the CI includes zero (+1.05 +-1.25, +0.42 +-1.56). The pairwise check's 0.97 less damage also has CI +-1.13, so it is not significant. (b) 'Opponents' creature counts identical (differences at most 0.1)' is slightly wrong: opponents have +0.13 +-0.07 more creatures at k8 against v5. Together with the max-power rise, this supports 'opposing boards grow larger'. (c) The suggested cause, more passes with castable cards, is contradicted per own turn. v5 casts as many spells per own turn as hs (+0.006 +-0.014) and passes with a cast available no more often (-0.042 +-0.047). Only the share of passes is higher (0.232 vs 0.175, because hs passes far more often overall: 3.28 vs 2.42 per own turn). The smaller board is therefore not explained by casting less. It more likely reflects what is cast and how creatures are traded or lost. The all-alive conditioning is post-treatment, but at k6 it keeps 96% of tables and the pairwise check agrees.
verdicts.correction: Compared on tables where all five candidates are alive, v5 holds +0.14 to +0.35 more cards (k6-k9). It has +0.5 to +1.1 more life at k6-7 (not significant later) and about 0.25 fewer creatures and 0.8-1.0 less power at k6-7. Opponents keep 1-3 more total life, and from k8 on their max power is 0.9-1.7 higher and their creature count +0.13 higher. v5 does not cast less per own turn than hs (casts +0.006 +-0.014; passes with a cast available -0.042 +-0.047), so 'more passes with castable cards' does not explain the gap.

verdicts.reason: The numbers reproduce and v3->v5 is significant on every tempo measure. Overreach in wording: (1) 'Every activity measure rose monotonically' is false. Permanents per own turn go 0.235 -> 0.228 -> 0.241. Commander casts are flat from v4b to v5 (0.141 -> 0.142). Only the v3->v5 endpoints were tested. (2) 'v3 ... dies a little less' than hs is null (-0.6 +-2.8 pts). (3) 'v3 passes with castable cards 46% more often than hs' holds per own turn (0.834/0.573). As a share of passes the gap is 0.311 vs 0.175. (4) On spending (casts, activations, commander casts, passes with a cast available), v5 already equals or exceeds hs. It trails hs only on board (creatures, power) and attackers. So v5 is not between v3 and hs on every tempo measure.
verdicts.correction: From v3 to v5, casts, activations, commander casts and attackers per own turn rose significantly (paired v5-v3: +0.05, +0.10, +0.019, +0.10). Passes with a cast available fell by 0.27 per own turn (-32%), and k6 board power rose by +0.80 +-0.21, with no loss of hand and a small life gain. Not every measure is monotone (permanents per turn dip at v4b; commander casts are flat from v4b to v5). v3 and hs differ in timing (v3 has 1.8 +-1.4 pts fewer wins before own turn 10) but not detectably in elimination rate.

verdicts.recomputed: Exits omit 'active' when it is seat 0; I default it to 0. Final blow = cause of the opponent exit(s) on the last elimination turn in candidate wins. Counted only when all of them were commander: hbot 42/396 (10.6%), hs 36/621 (5.8%), v3 58/619 (9.4%), v4b 67/675 (9.9%), v5 73/725 (10.1%). Counting any commander exit on that turn: hs 45/621 (7.2%), v5 81/725 (11.2%). Two-proportion z, hs vs v5: 2.47 under either definition (the claimed 38/621 and 77/725 give 2.95). Paired, per game, commander final blow: +2.25 +-1.22 pts. Commander casts per own turn: hs 0.123, v5 0.142 (paired +0.018 +-0.004). Commander-damage kills on the candidate's own turn per game: hs 0.062, v5 0.084 (paired +0.021 +-0.018). Opponent commander eliminations per game: hs 0.145 (232), v5 0.149. Candidate killed by commander: hs 49/938 (5.2%), v5 46/821 (5.6%). Stratified by own turns at the win (<=9 / 10-12 / >12): hs 17.3% (n=110) / 3.9% (282) / 6.6% (229); v5 13.4% (97) / 9.4% (318) / 12.3% (310). hs reweighted to v5's win-length mix: 6.8%. v5-only wins ending by commander: 47; hs-only: 18. Excess commander finishes, v5 minus hs: 37.
verdicts.reason: The direction holds and is not a game-length artefact (reweighting hs to v5's length mix gives 6.8%). Corrections: the counts (36/621 and 73/725, or 45/621 and 81/725 by definition), and z is about 2.5, not 2.9. The pattern is length-specific. In fast wins (<=9 own turns), hs finishes by commander damage more often than v5 (17.3% vs 13.4%, small n). The whole deficit comes from wins at 10+ own turns (3.9-6.6% vs 9.4-12.3%). So 'search underuses commander damage' applies to mid and long games only. '39 of v5's 104 extra wins end with a commander blow' is an accounting statement, not a causal one: it is simply the difference in commander finishes (37 by my count). It does not show those wins depend on commander damage. Net-feature visibility of commander damage is plausible but was not verified from the data. v3 finishes by commander almost as often as v5 (9.4%) with hs-level commander casts (0.124), so commander recasting alone is not the mechanism.
verdicts.correction: Candidate wins ending with a commander-damage blow: hs 36/621 (5.8%), v5 73/725 (10.1%), z about 2.5 (paired per game +2.25 +-1.22 pts). The gap is confined to wins after 10+ own turns (hs 3.9-6.6% vs v5 9.4-12.3%). In fast wins hs uses commander damage at least as often (17.3% vs 13.4%). v3 shows the same higher share with hs-level commander casting, so the extra commander casts (+0.018 +-0.004 per own turn) are not the whole explanation.

verdicts.recomputed: Candidate deck is identical across the 5 pilots on every table (asserted). Statistic: sum over decks of n_d*(mean_d - mean)^2 / var, over 45 decks with n = 7 to 50 games each. Observed 73.6, label-permutation null mean 43.7, p = 0.003 (2000 permutations). Split-half reliability r = 0.32 (500 splits). Deck-level correlations (permutation over decks): (v5-hs) vs (v4b-hbot) r = 0.34, p = 0.016; vs (v3-hbot) r = 0.28, p = 0.052. Terciles by hbot candidate win rate: weak 521 games (hbot 9.8%, hs 24.2 -> v5 32.1, +7.9 +-4.6); mid 547 (40.4 -> 47.5, +7.1 +-5.0); strong 532 (hbot 39.3%, 51.5 -> 56.0, +4.5 +-4.9). corr(gain, hbot rate) = -0.16, p = 0.29. corr(gain, hs rate) = -0.48. Covariates from hbot-pilot games: k6 creatures r = -0.35, p = 0.023; commander casts per own turn r = -0.33, p = 0.03; fast-win share r = -0.10, p = 0.54. Per-deck results reproduce: Upgrades Unleashed +0.30 (n=33), Reap the Tides +0.30 (30), Breed Lethality +0.29 (38), Hatsune Miku +0.26 (34), Most Wanted +0.24 (42), Blood Rites -0.31 +-0.17 (36; hs 0.83, v3 0.36, v4b 0.53, v5 0.53). Decks whose 95% normal CI excludes 0: 9 of 45 (about 2.3 expected by chance).
verdicts.reason: Heterogeneity, its partial repeat across nets, and the null strength relation all reproduce. Corrections: (1) Deck sizes are 7-50 games, not 23-50 (Calling All Angels has n=7). (2) 'Only 2 of 45 deck intervals exclude zero' does not reproduce. With unadjusted 95% intervals, 9 do (6 large gains plus Blood Rites and others), which is consistent with real heterogeneity. Perhaps the analyst applied a multiplicity correction without saying so. (3) corr with (v3-hbot) is borderline (p about 0.05). (4) The weak-vs-strong tercile difference (+7.9 vs +4.5) is itself not significant, so 'weak decks gain at least as much' is the most the data allows. (5) Blood Rites' loss is partly hs's own outlier (hs 0.83 vs hbot 0.33 and v4b/v5 0.53): the same regression-to-the-mean caveat the analyst raised for corr(gain, hs rate) applies to the largest single-deck loss. The covariate correlations (about -0.35, p about 0.02-0.03, 45 decks, several covariates tried) are suggestive. Read them as exploratory, not as an established mechanism.
verdicts.correction: Per-deck v5-hs gain is heterogeneous (permutation p = 0.003; split-half r = 0.32). It correlates with the v4b-hbot deck gain (r = 0.34, p = 0.016), and weakly with v3-hbot (r = 0.28, p = 0.05). It is unrelated to deck strength (r = -0.16, p = 0.29; tercile gains +7.9 / +7.1 / +4.5, differences n.s.). 9 of 45 unadjusted deck CIs exclude zero. The negative relation to board-centric decks (k6 creatures r = -0.35, commander casts r = -0.33) is exploratory. Blood Rites' -0.31 is partly an hs outlier.

verdicts.recomputed: Missing exit 'active' is read as seat 0. Last elimination on the candidate's own turn in its wins: hs 601/621 (96.8%), v5 711/725 (98.1%). Opponent eliminations on own turn per win: hs 2.07, v5 2.02. Candidate killed on its own turn: hs 3/938, v5 0/821. Candidate deaths on the eventual winner's turn: hs 0.596 (928), v5 0.635 (814). Stalled or failed: 3.2% vs 3.8%. All-alive opponent means at k4-k10: lands and hand |diff| <= 0.06, creature count +0.13 +-0.07 at k8 and +0.13 +-0.11 at k9 (otherwise <= 0.04). Own turns 1-4 (k4): life -0.03, lands +0.02 (v5-v3 life +0.11); power at k4 -0.20 +-0.07. Seat win rates (seats 0/1/2/3): hbot 22.1/27.0/21.1/28.6, hs 36.8/35.3/41.5/41.7, v3 32.1/37.5/41.5/43.7, v4b 39.6/40.4/42.0/46.7, v5 42.4/42.9/43.8/52.1. Seat counts 388-408.
