Without that, about 990 exits are mis-attributed and the 97% shrinks to 74%, so whoever relies on these numbers should note the encoding. Corrections: (1) Opponents' development is not entirely unchanged. At k8, opponents have +0.13 +-0.07 more creatures against v5, and their max power is higher by +0.90 +-0.53 (k8) and +1.66 +-0.91 (k9) (see finding 2). 'Differences of at most 0.11' is slightly wrong. (2) 'How games are closed' is unchanged in timing (own-turn finish rate) but not in method: commander-damage finishes nearly double (finding 4). (3) 'Every pilot does best in seat 3' is a tie for hs (41.7 vs 41.5 in seat 2). 'Deaths dealt by the winner' is really 'deaths on the winner's turn'.
verdicts.correction: Unchanged between hs and v5: the timing of the finishing blow (about 97-98% on the candidate's own turn), the rate of being killed on its own turn (<1%), the share of its deaths on the eventual winner's turn (0.60 vs 0.64), stall rate, and opponents' lands and hand size. Changed slightly: opponents' boards at k8+ (creatures +0.13 +-0.07, max power +0.9 to +1.7) and how often the final blow is commander damage (finding 4). Seat 3 is best or tied-best for every pilot. Seats are balanced, so this does not bias the comparison.

verdicts.recomputed: From the recomputations above: k6-8 all-alive v5-hs: hand +0.14 to +0.35, life +0.54 to +1.06 (significant at k6-7 only), power -0.77 to -1.02, opponent life +1.05 to +2.61. Eliminated -7.3 +-2.8 pts. Wins within 12 own turns +1.4 +-2.5 (with fewer than 12: +0.6 +-2.2). Wins after 12 own turns +5.1 +-2.3. v3->v5: k6 power +0.80 +-0.21, casts per own turn +5.4% (paired +0.051 +-0.013), pass_cast per own turn -32.5%, win steps +3.5 and +3.1. Per own turn, v5 vs hs: casts 1.023 vs 1.018 (paired +0.006 +-0.014), activations 0.844 vs 0.786, pass_cast 0.563 vs 0.573, attackers 1.326 vs 1.495 (-0.158 +-0.055). Attack-target shares (highest/middle/lowest life): hbot 42.4/28.5/29.1; by power 46.8/30.8/22.3.
verdicts.reason: As a synthesis it holds directionally, and every component number reproduces. One wording needs fixing. 'v5 sits between passive v3 and board-dumping hsearch on tempo' is true for board (creatures, power) and attacks. It is false for mana spending: v5 casts, activates and passes with a cast available at or above hs's level. So 'trades early board presence' should not imply it casts less. The hbot attack-target figures (42% highest life, 47% highest power) are hbot as the candidate pilot, assumed to carry over to hbot opponents, which is reasonable since the bot is the same. The alternative explanation (the net values hand more than the 2x weight) is untested here, as the analyst says. 'Wins after 12 own turns +5.1' carries a CI of +-2.3.
verdicts.correction: v5 matches or exceeds hsearch on mana spending (casts +0.006 +-0.014, activations +0.05, commander casts +0.018 per own turn). It deploys and attacks less: about 0.25 fewer creatures and 0.8 less power at k6, and -0.16 attackers per own turn. It keeps more cards and life, survives more (-7.3 pts eliminated), and wins its extra games after own turn 12 (+5.1 +-2.3 pts). On board and attacks it sits between v3 and hs. On spending it does not trail hs.

findings.claim: The network ranks positions much better than the hand-made leaf for every pilot and at every stage of the game. Once net_v is known, leaf_v adds almost no information about who wins. When the two disagree strongly, the network is the one that turns out right.
findings.evidence:
Snapshot-level AUC, network vs leaf: hbot 0.763 vs 0.667, hsearch 0.762 vs 0.680, v3 0.767 vs 0.675, v4b 0.767 vs 0.661, v5 0.750 vs 0.659. Log-loss: 0.497-0.599 for the network vs 0.746-0.899 for the leaf. Brier: 0.164-0.208 vs 0.220-0.262.
The network keeps its lead in every global-turn bin, by 0.06-0.15 AUC. For v5: turns 1-4 0.627 vs 0.546, turns 17-24 0.743 vs 0.651, turns 41-52 0.865 vs 0.751.
I fitted a logistic regression of won on logit(net) and logit(leaf) together. In v5 games the per-snapshot log-loss goes from 0.5797 with the network alone to 0.5793 with both. The coefficients are 0.78 for the network and 0.03 for the leaf; the standard deviations of the logits are 1.62 and 2.65. Results are the same for hbot (0.4881 to 0.4880) and hsearch (0.5603 to 0.5597).
In a 3x3 grid of tertiles, v5 games: inside the top leaf tertile, the observed win rate runs from 0.316 to 0.772 across network tertiles. Inside the top network tertile, it only runs from 0.654 to 0.772 across leaf tertiles.
Big disagreements, all pilots:
- Network above 0.6 and leaf below 0.2 (7,483 snapshots): the observed win rate is 0.66-0.74, close to the network's mean of 0.72.
- Network below 0.2 and leaf above 0.8 (1,731 snapshots): the observed win rate is 0.12-0.22, close to the network's mean of 0.11.
Correlation between the two values: 0.58-0.61 on the probability scale, 0.63-0.65 on the logit scale.
examples: v5 game 186, turn 33: candidate (seat 3, Tramplesaurus Rex) at 60 life, 7 creatures with 33 power. Seat 1 is at 10 life with 13 creatures and 49 power, and has taken 14 commander damage. Network 0.989, leaf 0.019. The candidate won that turn with commander damage.

v5 game 1247, turn 35, candidate's turn: candidate (Hatsune Miku) at 67 life with 9 creatures. The last opponent is at 7 life with 41 creatures and 64 power. Network 0.991, leaf 0.000. The candidate won that turn.
v5 game 610, turn 31: candidate (seat 1, Tinker Time) has 13 creatures and 26 power but only 7 life, against a 49-life seat 2. Network 0.012, leaf 0.997. The candidate died on turn 32.

hbot game 486, turn 22: candidate (Wakanda Forever CE) at 17 life with 14 creatures and 32 power, against two 40-life opponents with 29 and 7 power. Network 0.005, leaf 0.998. The candidate died on turn 25.
hbot game 1500, turn 24: candidate (Keen Engineering) has 10 creatures vs at most 3 for any opponent, but 24 life vs opponents at 40/40/42. Network 0.006, leaf 0.994. It lost, on turn 48.
findings.interpretation: Most of what the leaf knows is contained in the network, which also takes the leaf as an input. The network's lead is not confined to one stage. The leaf's calibration slope is only 0.21-0.25 (logistic recalibration won ~ a + b*logit(leaf)), so its logits are about 4-5 times too extreme. That matters for PUCT because the exploration term is sized to the value scale. A leaf that saturates near 0 or 1 in 37% of snapshots (below 0.1 or above 0.8) leaves the search little to tell children apart.

findings.claim: I confirmed the miscalibration. The network over-estimates the candidate in hbot games and under-estimates it in every search pilot's games, worst in v5 games. Its predictions are roughly calibrated for a pilot of about 30-35% strength. This is what you get from a state-only value trained mostly on the searched seat with 15% random moves and an older network, mixed with unmarked hbot-style data. The bias is largest early in the game, before the board shows how strong the pilot is.
findings.evidence:
Per-pilot quintiles of net_v, predicted vs observed:
- hbot: 0.057/0.056, 0.190/0.159, 0.289/0.234, 0.404/0.327, 0.675/0.586
- hsearch: middle quintile 0.327/0.389
- v4b: middle quintile 0.349/0.432
- v5: 0.104/0.178, 0.251/0.378, 0.363/0.474, 0.518/0.580, 0.806/0.814
So the task's claim (0.35 predicted vs 0.49 observed) is roughly right for v5. But hbot games are not calibrated: the network over-predicts them by about 5 points.
With one weight per game, mean prediction vs observed: hbot 0.314 vs 0.247, hsearch 0.359 vs 0.388, v3 0.369 vs 0.387, v4b 0.380 vs 0.422, v5 0.397 vs 0.453.
Recalibration intercept with the slope fixed at 1, in logit units: hbot -0.31, v3 +0.20, hsearch +0.26, v4b +0.34, v5 +0.42. That is the same order as pilot strength. The free slope is 0.81-0.88 for every pilot.
Across pilots the network's mean moves only 0.083 (0.314 to 0.397) while the observed rate moves 0.206. The board states carry roughly 40% of the difference in pilot strength.
Training shards: the marked seat won 33.1% of seat-games in data/v4 (explore 0.15 with v3) and 35.5% in data/v5 (explore 0.15 with v4b). The unmarked data/v3 (ehbot:0.15, all seats) has a rate of 25.6%. All three are far below v5's 45.3% in the arena.
Early-game prior: the turn-1 net_v is bit-identical for all five pilots on the same table (mean 0.281; maximum difference between hbot and v5 is 0). The turns 1-8 mean is 0.301-0.303 for every pilot. That equals the record-weighted label rate of all three training sets at turns 1-8, which is 0.300 (v3: 0.250 on 682k records; v4: 0.331; v5: 0.355). It is below the 0.343 of the marked sets.
Observed minus predicted in v5 games by turn bin: +0.150 (turns 1-8), +0.109 (9-16), +0.052 (17-24), +0.031 (25-32), +0.032 (33-48), +0.068 (49+). In hbot games: -0.053, -0.072, -0.067, -0.047, -0.015, +0.023.
examples: Turn 1 of every table: the network gives the same value whoever pilots the seat (mean 0.281), yet the candidate's final win rate is 24.8% with hbot and 45.3% with v5.
findings.interpretation:
The network maps state to win probability, averaged over whatever pilot produced its training data. It cannot see that the pilot is now stronger, except through better boards later on. The 15% random moves and the previous network made the training pilot about 10 points weaker than v5 in the arena. That alone accounts for most of the offset.
The early prior of 0.30 matches the pooled base rate including the unmarked v3 data. This suggests the 'mark' input barely moves the early-game prior; I infer that from base rates and did not evaluate the network on its training shards.
For move choice, a roughly uniform logit shift is harmless, because siblings in a search share a turn and a pilot. The slope of 0.81-0.88 and the stage-dependent shift could matter for PUCT exploration scaling and for any future use of absolute values, such as resign rules or mixing with the leaf.
Alternatives considered: deck effects cannot explain it because tables are paired across pilots. Survivorship affects the turn bins but not the turn-1 identity.

findings.claim: The network values the number of living opponents about the way the outcomes do. The leaf largely ignores it, because it compares against the strongest opponent only and maps 'equal score' to 0.5 even with three opponents alive. The network also, correctly, likes being at the start of its own turn; the leaf, wrongly, dislikes it.
findings.evidence:
I ran a regression on 17 table features (own and opponent life, hand, lands, creatures and power, commander damage received, living opponents, turn, active). It has three targets: logit(net) by OLS, logit(leaf) by OLS with the leaf clipped to ±6, and the outcome by logistic regression.
Coefficient per additional living opponent, in logit units, network / leaf / outcome: hbot -0.56/+0.03/-0.51, hsearch -0.59/-0.09/-0.65, v5 -0.46/-0.25/-0.48.
Binned by living opponents (3/2/1), v5 games:
- leaf 0.399/0.427/0.552
- network 0.371/0.505/0.639
- observed 0.456/0.546/0.688
hbot games: leaf 0.363/0.336/0.471, network 0.305/0.352/0.478, observed 0.243/0.329/0.510.
Snapshots with the leaf near parity (0.44-0.56): 97% have 3 opponents alive. They win 0.266 (hbot) and 0.477 (v5), where the network says 0.317 and 0.337. AUC within the 3-opponent snapshots, network vs leaf: 0.709-0.731 vs 0.623-0.653.
Active (snapshot at the start of the candidate's own turn), network / leaf / outcome: hbot +0.16/-0.14/+0.25, hsearch +0.19/-0.15/+0.27, v5 +0.10/-0.16/+0.24.
examples: hbot game 1410, turn 39, candidate's turn: one opponent left at 11 life, who has taken 18 commander damage from the candidate. The candidate is at 61 life with 1 creature against the opponent's 10 creatures. Network 0.977, leaf 0.008. The candidate won that turn.
v5 game 1517, turn 46: two opponents dead, candidate at 10 life with 6 creatures, last opponent at 2 life with 16 creatures. Network 0.983, leaf 0.000. The candidate won.
findings.interpretation:
A multiplayer value should rise as opponents are eliminated and should account for the tempo of having the next turn. The leaf's two-player sigmoid does neither. This is one concrete thing the network has learned that the leaf cannot express. A plausible link to play is that it rewards finishing off weak opponents rather than racing material.
The sign on 'active' may partly reflect the snapshot timing: the active player has just untapped and drawn. Both the network and the outcomes agree that it is good, which makes the leaf's negative sign an error.

findings.claim: The leaf prices board material, especially creature count, at many times what it is worth relative to life. The network's exchange rates are close to the ones implied by the outcomes. Most big disagreements are boards that look strong to the leaf but not to the network: wide token or artifact boards, with the candidate low on life and taking commander damage. In the reverse case the candidate is healthy and the opponents have big boards but low life.
findings.evidence:
Exchange rates from the same regressions: feature coefficient divided by the own-life coefficient, in life points, network / leaf / outcome.
- Own creature: hbot 1.8/8.9/1.8, hsearch 3.0/17.5/2.3, v5 1.8/7.7/1.8
- Own land: 2.0/6.0/2.0, 2.8/9.5/1.6, 2.4/3.8/1.3
- Opponents' mean creature count: hbot -1.3/-9.9/-0.5, hsearch -2.9/-17.5/-1.7, v5 -2.4/-11.5/-1.1
The leaf's actual formula is 3 per land and 10 + 2*(power+toughness) per creature, against 1 per life point.
The 'net low, leaf high' snapshots, compared with all snapshots of that pilot:
- own creatures 7.5 vs 1.8 (hbot) and 6.0 vs 2.1 (v5)
- own life 23.9 vs 36.0 and 30.5 vs 37.1
- commander damage received 2.1 vs 0.4-0.5
- on the candidate's own turn only 14-15% of the time vs 28%
They cluster in go-wide decks. Per 1000 snapshots: Wakanda Forever CE 43, Wakanda Forever 33, Keen Engineering 30, against an average of 5.6. Those three decks account for 32% of all such snapshots.
The 'net high, leaf low' snapshots: own life 39 vs 36-37, the strongest opponent has 6.5-6.8 creatures and 18-20 power, the weakest opponent's life is 19 vs 30-32, and 2.35 opponents are alive. They are concentrated in Breed Lethality, First Flight and Hatsune Miku at 56-87 per 1000.
Null results:
- Opponents' life: the sum of the three opponent-life coefficients relative to own life is -0.55/-0.71/-1.18 (hbot), -1.19/-2.08/-0.69 (hsearch) and -0.88/-0.56/-1.03 (v5). No consistent difference between network and leaf.
- Hand size: weakly valued by everything (network 0.6-0.65 life per card in hbot and v5 games; outcome between -0.03 and 0.61).
- Commander damage received: the network penalises it (-1.7 to -3.0 life per point). The outcome coefficient is unstable across pilots (-3.4, -1.05, -0.04), so I make no claim about it.
examples: v5 game 145, turn 37: candidate (Mirror Mastery) has 19 creatures but only 12 power and 15 life, against 31- and 40-life opponents with 24 and 17 power. Network 0.013, leaf 0.992. It died on turn 39.
hbot game 320, turn 42: candidate (Wakanda Forever) at 10 life with 26 creatures and 30 power, facing a 41-life opponent. Network 0.002, leaf 1.000. It died on turn 43.
v5 game 1325, turn 36: candidate at 55 life with 1 creature; seat 1 has 16 creatures and 36 power but only 16 life. Network 0.972, leaf 0.000. The candidate won on turn 40.
hbot game 697, turn 65: candidate at 42 life with 2 creatures, against seat 2 at 29 life with 11 creatures (6 power) and seat 1 at 11 life. Network 0.977, leaf 0.000. The candidate won on turn 70.
findings.interpretation:
With 10 points per creature regardless of size, a board of 1/1 tokens dominates the leaf's score. The network has learned that such boards often lose, and from the deck features it knows which decks produce them.
The regressions are linear on collinear features, so I trust the large, consistent ratios but not the individual small coefficients. The 4-10x over-valuation of creature count by the leaf shows up in all three pilots and in the binned profiles.

findings.claim: From turn 1 the network already knows deck matchups about as well as a deck win-rate table. It ranks eventual winners correctly about 2 rounds (8-12 global turns) earlier than the leaf. Deck identity explains only a small part of its lead.
findings.evidence:
AUC at turn 1, network vs leaf: 0.614-0.634 vs 0.535-0.549. For comparison, the candidate deck's win rate from the hbot tables, leaving the table out, gives AUC 0.621-0.641, and own minus strongest opponent deck gives 0.625-0.653. Correlation between turn-1 net_v and deck strength: 0.44.
Across the 45 decks, correlation of mean net_v with observed win rate: 0.933, vs 0.671 for the leaf. Examples: Aura of Courage, network 0.204 / leaf 0.320 / observed 0.114; Calling All Angels, 0.588 / 0.531 / 0.782.
Within-deck AUC for v5, weighted by snapshots: network 0.728, leaf 0.658. The pooled values are 0.750 and 0.659, so deck identity is worth about 0.02 of the 0.09 lead.
AUC by turns before game end, network vs leaf:
- v5: 0-3 turns 0.937/0.873, 4-7 0.880/0.800, 8-11 0.827/0.723, 12-15 0.780/0.661, 16-23 0.731/0.614, 24-31 0.671/0.570
- hbot: 0.942/0.880, 0.876/0.795, 0.828/0.747, 0.777/0.694, 0.744/0.635
The network at 16-23 turns before the end matches the leaf at 8-11 turns before.
Lock-in for eventual winners, after per-pilot recalibration: the turn from which p stays above 0.5 until the end. v5: median 18 global turns before the end for the network vs 7 for the leaf (means 18.8 vs 10.2); 6% never lock with the network vs 19% with the leaf. hbot: median 6 vs 2. hsearch: 12 vs 5.
examples: hbot game 912: Keen Engineering (seat 1) eventually won. At turn 26 seat 1 had 22 creatures; the candidate (seat 0) was at 29 life with 0 creatures. Network 0.014, leaf 1.000, measured for the candidate. The candidate died on turn 28. (The leaf_v of 1.000 here, with no creatures and lower life, looks odd; it may reflect permanents not in the snapshot or an artefact, and is worth checking.)
findings.interpretation:
The lock-in measure depends on the base rate. For losers it is dominated by the low recalibrated values, so I report it for winners only. The time-to-end AUC curves are the cleaner evidence.
Deck knowledge is legitimate information for a value function, but it explains only a minority of the network's advantage. The rest comes from reading the board, as in the findings on living opponents and on material.

findings.claim: The pilots' own searches shape the positions they reach. hsearch games are full of positions the leaf likes and the network does not, and the network pilots reach positions the network likes and the leaf does not. The leaf shows the over-optimism expected from an optimiser exploiting its errors (optimizer's curse) in hsearch's own games. The network does not show the same in the network pilots' games.
findings.evidence:
Share of snapshots with the network above 0.6 and the leaf below 0.2: hbot 1.45%, hsearch 1.42%, v3 2.66%, v4b 3.21%, v5 3.27%. With the network below 0.2 and the leaf above 0.8: 0.71%, 1.13%, 0.32%, 0.33%, 0.33%.
Mean net_v minus leaf_v: hbot -0.044, hsearch -0.084, v3/v4b/v5 -0.006 to -0.007. Mean leaf: hsearch 0.451 vs hbot 0.367; mean network: 0.368 vs 0.323.
Leaf recalibration intercepts for two pilots of equal strength, hsearch (38.8%) and v3 (38.7%): -0.317 vs -0.163. The leaf over-predicts more, by about 0.15 logit, in the games of the pilot that maximises it.
The network intercept is largest in v5 games (+0.42), so it is not over-optimistic there. In v5 games, positions with the network high and the leaf low still win at 0.723.
findings.interpretation:
The selection effect is expected: each search pushes the game toward states its evaluator scores highly. Because the network's high values hold up in its own games, its errors are apparently not being exploited at 25 simulations. The leaf's errors do appear to be exploited by hsearch.
The comparison between equally strong pilots is a single pair, and the 0.15-logit gap has no confidence interval, hence medium confidence.

findings.claim: Null result: whether the network and the leaf disagree about the current position predicts only weakly whether v5 and hsearch choose different actions there. Action differences come from how children are compared, not from the value of the root position.
findings.evidence:
I used the probes file, 55,706 v5 decisions with an hsearch alternative. Disagreement is measured as the percentile of net_v minus the percentile of leaf_v.
- Priority decisions: v5 and hsearch agree on 0.678 where the absolute difference is below 0.1 (n=13,065) and on 0.658 where it is above 0.3 (n=4,682). Self-agreement is 1.000 in both cases.
- By signed difference from -1 to +1: 0.712, 0.721, 0.678, 0.643, 0.615. The pilots agree a little less where the network rates the position above the leaf.
- Attackers: 0.635 vs 0.621 (self-agreement 0.843/0.862). Blockers: 0.635 vs 0.580 (self 0.875/0.822). Targets: 0.470 vs 0.464.
- By net_v at priority decisions: agreement 0.695-0.720 for net_v below 0.6, falling to 0.638 at 0.6-0.9 and 0.606 above 0.9. The pilots diverge most when v5 thinks it is winning.
findings.interpretation: Root-level disagreement is a poor proxy for where the evaluators lead the search apart. Studying play differences would need child-level values, meaning both evaluators applied to the options at a decision, which this data does not contain. The lower agreement in winning positions fits the network's use of eliminations and tempo (the finding on living opponents), but these data cannot show what causes it.

open_questions: Does the 'mark' input actually shift the network's prior? The turns 1-8 output of 0.30 equals the pooled label rate including unmarked v3 data. Evaluating models/v5.caiv on held-out data/v5 records by turn would settle whether the mark is weak or the early v5 records are too few (4.9% of records are from turns 1-8).

Would a calibration fix help search strength? Options: recalibrating against the playing pilot's strength, training only on non-exploring searched-seat games, or a value per living opponent instead of a scalar. The constant logit offset should not change move ranking, but the slope of 0.81-0.88 and the stage-dependent bias interact with the PUCT exploration constant.

Child-level values are needed to see which candidate actions the two evaluators rank differently. Logging net and leaf values for each root child at probed decisions would turn the material, elimination and tempo findings into specific play decisions.

Some snapshots have leaf_v near 1.0 for a seat with no creatures and lower life (e.g. hbot game 912, turn 30-34, after the candidate died, where leaf_v stays 1.000). Check how leaf_v and net_v are recorded for seats near elimination, and whether the snapshot's 'lost' flag lags the engine's FeatLost.

Does the network's dislike of go-wide token decks (Wakanda, Keen Engineering, Tinker Time) reflect real weakness under this kernel, or the roughly 15 cards per deck replaced by basic lands hollowing out those decks? Check per-deck results against the replacement lists.

verdicts.reason: Every headline number reproduces once snapshots after the candidate's elimination are removed. The direction holds for every pilot and every stage, and the effect is far larger than any noise between games. The quoted v5 examples (games 186, 1247 and 610) and hbot 486/1500 match the data. Two caveats, neither of which changes the verdict. First, the net takes the leaf as an input, so the leaf adding nothing once the net is known is partly true by construction. Second, the logit SDs (1.62/2.65) and the leaf slope depend on how logit(0) and logit(1) are clipped; the leaf's SD ranges from 2.7 to 3.5.

verdicts.correction: (1) The per-opponent regression coefficients (net/leaf/outcome about -0.5/0/-0.5) depend on how dead opponents' life is coded. With mean and min life over living opponents I reproduce them: hbot -0.56/+0.02/-0.51, hsearch -0.59/-0.08/-0.65, v5 -0.46/-0.26/-0.48. Coding dead opponents' life as 0 (sorted), or summing living life, flips the sign: hbot +0.33/+0.20/+0.01, v5 +0.26/+0.06/+0.19. Use only the binned evidence. (2) The leaf does not ignore eliminations; it under-weights them. From 3 to 1 living opponents the leaf rises +0.11 (hbot) and +0.15 (v5). The observed rate rises +0.27 and +0.23, the net +0.17 and +0.27. So the leaf captures roughly 40-65% of the observed rise. (3) 'The leaf wrongly dislikes being active' is an artefact. The leaf has no input for whose turn it is. Within the 3-opponent snapshots the leaf's active coefficient is -0.00 to +0.05. There the net's is +0.03 to +0.11 and the outcome's +0.13 to +0.25. Corrected claim: the leaf has no notion of tempo, and the net gives a small positive premium, smaller than the outcome regression implies. The pooled negative leaf coefficient comes from mixing snapshot types: with fewer opponents alive the candidate is active more often (50% with one opponent left vs 25%).

verdicts.correction: (1) Formula: the leaf scores 3 per land, 10 per other non-land permanent, plus 2*(power+toughness) for a creature (third_party/gorge/dirac/search/eval.go). Artifact and enchantment tokens such as Treasures and Clues count 10 each, which strengthens the go-wide/artifact reading. (2) 'The network's exchange rates are close to the outcome's' holds for hbot, v5 and roughly hsearch only. Own creature, net vs outcome: v3 0.86 vs 1.32, v4b 2.61 vs 0.07. Opponents' creature count in v4b: net -6.84 vs outcome +0.34. Restrict the claim to those three pilots, or call the outcome ratios unstable. (3) Wakanda Forever and Wakanda Forever Collector's Edition are essentially the same deck, so the clustering covers two archetypes, not three decks.

Its leaf of 1.000 is therefore what the formula gives, and the candidate WON while the net said 0.014 at turn 26. It is a counterexample to the net, not an oddity of the leaf. Drop it or present it as a net miss. (2) Lock-in, same definition, recalibrated per pilot. v5: net median 18 (mean 19.0) vs leaf 9 (11.6). hbot: 6 vs 3. hsearch: 13 vs 7. The never-lock shares (6% vs 19%) reproduce. Without recalibration the gaps shrink to 13 vs 8, 9 vs 7 and 11 vs 9, so the metric depends on the threshold. Rely on the time-to-end AUC curves. 'Deck identity explains only a small part' holds for ranking within the training pool, but should not be read as saying deck familiarity is unimportant for play.
